title: Is Jesus the God of the Bible?
summary: Historical sources indicate that the full divinity of Jesus wasn’t the creation of a fourth-century church council but a fundamental belief of Christians from the beginning.
content: There’s a long-standing scholarly debate about how early Christians viewed Jesus’s identity. Was he merely a righteous man? Was he a man “exalted” to a divine status? Or did they think he was really God in the flesh? In this second of a two-part session from TGC25 (watch part 1 ), Michael Kruger explores the Christology of the earliest Christian movement, drawing on both New Testament texts and second-century patristic sources. These historical sources indicate that the full divinity of Jesus wasn’t the creation of a fourth-century church council but a fundamental belief of Christians from the beginning. In This Episode 00:08 – The scholarly debate on Jesus 08:22 – Jesus as God in the New Testament 11:22 – Pauline evidence for high Christology 11:35 – Monotheism and 1 Corinthians 25:10 – Worship in second-century Christianity 31:42 – Early scribal traditions and names Resources Mentioned: Christianity at the Crossroads by Michael J. Kruger The Epistle to Diognetus SIGN UP for one of our newsletters to stay informed about TGC’s latest resources. Help The Gospel Coalition renew and unify the contemporary church in the ancient gospel: Give today . Don’t miss an episode of The Gospel Coalition Podcast : Apple Podcasts Spotify YouTube
author: Michael J. Kruger

title: Mordecai: Joseph 2.0
summary: Joseph’s life and service to the kingdom of God in the book of Genesis serve as a foreshadowing type of Mordecai’s life and service.
content: The world of computer programming has provided multiple examples of software “updates” that were inferior to their predecessors. Microsoft followed up the incredible success of Windows XP with two infamous failures: the Windows Vista and Windows 8 operating systems, both hated by users. The significant blow to Microsoft’s reputation serves as a reminder us that “Version 2.0” does not always represent an advance over a predecessor. The Bible, though, often depicts its characters as “new” versions of earlier heroes, a phenomenon known as typology —an earlier “type” is a foreshadowing of a later “antitype.” The most obvious example is the New Testament’s presentation of Jesus as the perfect “Version 2.0” of Old Testament figures. Paul calls Jesus “the second man” (1 Cor. 15:47), in contrast to Adam, who was a “type of the one who was to come” (Rom. 5:14). Jesus, the “son of David,” is so superior to his kingly forefather that even David himself had to address him as “Lord” in Psalm 110 (see Matt. 22:41–45). Melchizedek, the priest-king of ancient Jerusalem in Genesis 14, prefigured the work of Jesus, a priest and king superior to all who came before him (Heb. 5:1–10; 6:19–20; 7:1–28). The New Testament employs typology to instruct the church about God’s redemptive plan and, above all, about the Redeemer. We sometimes fail to realize that the Old Testament also uses typology to present its own heroes as “Version 2.0” of an earlier figure. Let’s consider the book of Esther’s depiction of Mordecai as a kind of “second Joseph.” By doing so, we will see how this Old Testament book speaks about Jesus Christ (Luke 24:44). How Is Joseph a ‘Type’ of Mordecai? Mordecai’s life and service to the Persian king Ahasuerus (Xerxes) is remarkably similar to Joseph’s service to Pharaoh. Just as Joseph was taken against his will to live in a foreign land (Gen. 37:12–36), so also Mordecai lived as an exile in the Persian capital of Susa (Est. 2:5–6). While both men eventually rose to second in ruling power (Gen. 41:40; Est. 10:3), both experienced hardship and humiliation along the way (Gen. 39–40; Est. 4:1–17). The New Testament employs typology to instruct the church about God’s redemptive plan and, above all, about the Redeemer. When Pharaoh placed Joseph in power “over all the land of Egypt,” he gave him the royal “signet ring” that was on his own hand, just as Ahasuerus gave the “signet ring” he wore on his hand to Mordecai (Gen. 41:41–42; Est. 8:2; cf. 3:10). Pharaoh exalted Joseph by dressing him in fine clothes and making him ride in a royal chariot preceded by a crier (Gen. 41:42–43); similarly, Ahasuerus ordered that Mordecai also be dressed in royal clothes, mounted on the king’s horse, and led in procession to proclamations of the king’s favor (Est. 6:9, 11). Ironically, this exaltation was the idea of the villain Haman. The striking similarities between these two Old Testament heroes lead us to respond like Bernie Kropp in The Incredibles : “ Coincidence? I think not!” What’s at Stake? By presenting Mordecai as “Joseph 2.0,” the author of Esther helps the reader to understand what’s at stake in the narrative. Behind the scenes, it was the Lord who had providentially sent Joseph to Egypt to preserve the lives of many, including a “remnant” of the sons of Israel (Gen. 45:5–8). While the book of Esther has a “secular” appearance on the surface because it never explicitly mentions God, we can see the Lord’s providential hand at work in bringing Mordecai to a position of rule and authority. In the end, the Lord uses Mordecai (as he did Joseph) as an agent of salvation for many people, both Jew and Gentile (Gen. 41:53–57; Est. 8:17; 9:3; 9:27; 10:3). Just consider for a moment that if Haman were to succeed in exterminating “the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus” (Est. 3:6), it would extinguish the Davidic house and thereby prevent the coming of Jesus, the Son of David (see Rev. 12:1–6). What Can We Learn? Joseph’s
author: Max Rogland

title: ‘I Was a Child of War’: How to Help Abuse Survivors Understand the Past
summary: Yes, we were weak, but we were warriors, not victims.
content: I grew up in a violent home, and it took me decades to find terms and categories that finally let me understand that aspect of my childhood. My first conversation partners and readings said I was a victim of abuse, but that framing was too passive to resonate with me. I believe the passive voice is valid, even essential. But when I discovered another framework, the child of war, I finally began to understand my past. Personal History That Led to Thoughts of War My father was a gifted professional, a compelling speaker who also possessed a shrewd wisdom. My mother seemed like a match—gifted, educated, and kind. But he was violent, even though for 16 years he was a pastor, and my mother couldn’t contain him. His behavior was our family secret, and if I hoped to understand it, I was on my own. Eventually, I read stories about one-dimensional moral monsters called “abusers”; their children were “victims.” But my parents seemed too admirable to be monsters, and the idea that I was a passive victim didn’t label my experience. I left home at 16 and essentially forgot the past until the month my father died. At that point, my readings on war let me see that my childhood had much in common with people who tried to resist and endure the aggression of a superior power. Terms like “resistance,” “war,” and “agency” fit better. They fostered understanding and healing. My first sharp memory is as ragged as a torn fingernail. Four years old, I’m hiding in my mother’s closet, behind dresses that smell of dust and skin cream. My skin stings and a deep ache runs beneath the surface. I’ve been spanked enough to know how it feels, but this is different. I think, I did something wrong, but what? I must deserve this, but why did he hit me so hard? Why does it hurt . . . so . . . much? I’m baffled by what we call mistreatment and betrayal. Fifty years later, I realized that 4-year-olds shouldn’t have the ability or experience to reflect critically on their beatings. And yet, because I could judge his actions, I could separate myself from him—he was “the” father rather than “my” father—and that gave me agency. When I turned 7, my favorite birthday gift was a miniature cowboy wagon. It was cheap, and the father quickly detected a flaw in the plastic. “This will snap,” he declared. He tugged and pulled at it until it broke, then he handed me the pieces and said, “See, I told you that would happen.” The playground had taught me that this was cruelty, so I decided to feel nothing , to sever his capacity to wound me. It was a foolish vow, one no child can fully keep, but it gave me a sense of agency or control. Two years later, it paid off. The chief gift for my 9th birthday was a basketball. When he decided I liked it too much, he stabbed it with a long knife. But by then, I’d hardened myself enough (agency again) to feel no grief, no surprise. It registered as a problem: Where would I get the money to buy another ball? How would I keep it safe? Because I could judge my father’s actions, I could separate myself from him, and that gave me agency. As time passed, my older brother and I began to resist him. We wore thick jeans when it seemed a belt might begin to fly. If a blow landed? Physical pain usually doesn’t last long. Social pains were tougher. The family moved often, because the father could always get a job but was too erratic to keep one. I attended five schools in seven years, chiefly in insular towns. I discovered that my athletic skills let me make friends through one team or another. Yet it was wise to mask my academic abilities-—unless the boys needed a math champion to wipe the smirks off the smart girls’ faces. I was making a way, until the dynamics at home shifted. Perhaps it was the alcohol. Perhaps it was the professional failure. The father was now reduced to the oversight of a tiny country church, two part-time jobs, and summer work for the Red Cross. Whatever the reasons, his behavior became ominous. He cursed and raged day after day,
author: Dan Doriani

title: Caring Well at Both Ends of Life (with Jen Wilkin)
summary: Melissa and Courtney talk with Jen Wilkin about how seeing the parallels between the beginning of life and its end can help us care for aging loved ones with compassion and honor.
content: Melissa and Courtney talk with Jen Wilkin about how seeing the parallels between the beginning of life and its end can help us care for aging loved ones with compassion and honor. They discuss how our culture’s prioritization of self-sufficiency poorly prepares us for the day when we’ll need to accept help. They share their stories of caring for aging parents and talk about how they’re seeking to number their own days aright as they age. Resources Mentioned: Dust to Dust by Jen Wilkin We Shall All Be Changed by Whitney Pipkin Being Mortal by Atul Gawande Related Resources: 5 Ways to Honor an Aging Loved One (Even When It’s Hard) The Joy of Caring for Aging Parents Caregivers Suffer from Dementia Too Honor Your Father and Mother Discussion Questions: 1. Have you ever cared for someone during a season of significant need, or have you received that care? How did the experience shape your understanding of dependence on others? 2. Why can it be difficult to receive help from others, even when we know we need it? What does our reluctance to depend on others reveal about us? 3. Our culture often measures a person’s worth by his or her productivity or abilities. How does the gospel challenge those assumptions, especially as we age? 4. When we think about the possibility of losing some of our independence and abilities as we age, what truths about God and our identity in Christ give us hope? 5. How can churches help ensure that older adults (especially those without children or nearby family) are known and cared for? 6. What practices or habits do you want to cultivate to help you age well, both physically and spiritually?
author: Courtney Doctor, Melissa Kruger, Jen Wilkin

title: Lessons from Ezra on Leading a Story You Didn’t Start
summary: Ezra entered a story God had already begun. Ezra teaches leaders how to continue God’s work in the lives of his people.
content: In the book of Ezra, Ezra doesn’t even appear until chapter 7. That means more than half the book unfolds before the man for whom it’s named ever steps onto the scene. That observation stayed with me long after our sermon series in the book ended. The more I reflected on it, the more it resonated with my experience of leadership. Ezra isn’t a leadership manual; the book’s primary purpose is to highlight God’s sovereignty and his steadfast commitment to carrying out his redemptive purposes in and through his people. But if we pay attention to how God uses Ezra in his ministry context, there is a word here to those called to lead stories they didn’t start. Story Ezra Entered Long before Ezra arrives, the Jewish exiles hear about the possibility of homecoming through King Cyrus’s decree, fulfilling the Word of the Lord spoken through Jeremiah (chap. 1). Stirred by the Spirit, they leave the lives they had grown accustomed to and journey home to Jerusalem (chap. 2). The rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem begins, and when its foundation is completed, the exiles’ pent-up emotions erupt into shouts of joy and sorrow that could barely be distinguished from one another (chap. 3). Unexpected opposition then halts the rebuilding (chap. 4), but through a series of providential circumstances, the work resumes, and the temple is finally completed after a long journey of uncertainty (chap. 5–6). This story is already filled with so many layers: stirring of the Spirit, risk, courage, failure, emotions, disappointment, uncertainty, sovereignty, grace. Every chapter seems to beg for more stories to be told. The point is simple yet profound: Before Ezra ever leads, God is already at work. A story is already underway. Ezra 1–6 isn’t an extended introduction, as though everything before chapter 7 were simply a prelude to Ezra’s ministry. Rather, in God’s timing, Ezra is brought into a story far larger than himself. The same is true for many leaders today who inherit a story they didn’t start. Every church carries memories of joy and sorrow, faithfulness and failure, growth and disappointment. Every congregation has a history that inevitably shapes its present. Wise leaders recognize that they aren’t beginning God’s work; they’re joining it. Story Ezra Continued What, then, can Ezra show us about leading a story we didn’t start? Here are four lessons. 1. Pray first. When King Artaxerxes commissions Ezra to guide and teach God’s people who have returned to Jerusalem, Ezra prepares to enter this story by calling those traveling with him to fast and pray. Rather than relying on military protection to get him safely to Jerusalem, he turns to trusting in God’s provision and protection (chap. 7–8). Notice how quickly Ezra turns to prayer. Prayer positions our minds and hearts to actively walk in the reality that the story ultimately doesn’t depend on us. Do you have a habit of praying? Pause often and pray something even as simple as this: “Lord, go before me and help me join where you are and what you’re doing.” Prayer reminds us who is ultimately going before us to build up his people. 2. Expect heartbreak. In Ezra 9, after beginning his teaching ministry and seeking spiritual renewal among the people, Ezra learns that God’s people have fallen into serious covenant unfaithfulness. His response is surprising: He tears his garments, pulls out his hair, and falls before God. His first response isn’t outrage: Why is this happening now? I just started my new role! It’s not damage control: How bad is the situation, and what are my immediate action items? And it’s not blame shifting: This problem predates me. Thank God I’m not responsible for this! Prayer positions our minds and hearts to actively walk in the reality that the story ultimately doesn’t depend on us. Ezra’s instinctive and immediate response is grief. Many leaders enter into new churches and ministry contexts hoping to teach, mentor, cast new vision, and build something impressive and influen
author: Benjamin Bae

title: When Families Sit Together in Church: The Missional Opportunity
summary: The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity.
content: Most pastors I know are working on a common problem: How do we better serve the people who come to church and feel like everyone has a family group and no one is genuinely welcoming? In a recent article , Dave Moore argues that for the sake of the Great Commission, you should stop sitting with your family at church. He writes that “church is for others” and says we should think of our church attendance in terms of deployment for mission. The article appeared on The Gospel Coalition’s Australian site. TGC’s international coalitions have their own independent editorial teams. All agree to publish resources that align with TGC’s Foundation Documents , but individual writers , staff members , and Council members often disagree on matters that fall outside our Confessional Statement and Theological Vision for Ministry. In this case, I respectfully disagree with Moore. Any church committed to reaching lost people and including outsiders is asking themselves how to best address the problems of cliques and people not feeling like they belong. But when Moore says that “dividing ourselves for the sake of others is the most beautiful picture of Christian unity,” I believe he overstates his case. The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity. More than that, to present family members worshiping together as an obstacle to love for others neglects the mission of the family and God’s call to parents. Acknowledging legitimate situations where families can’t or don’t sit together in church, as Christians, we don’t choose between our families or our mission. Building gospel-centered families is Great Commission ministry. Families as Mission God commands parents to teach his words and ways diligently to their children (Deut. 6:7). We’re called to train up our children in the way they should go (Prov. 22:6). The Bible places a priority on the family as a first-order love over against providing for others (1 Tim. 5:8). The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity. The primary responsibility for showing children “the way they should go” belongs to the parents, not the people of God in the abstract (Gen. 18:19). Parents set the tone for the worshipful commitment of a household (Josh. 24:15). Parents are the generation that proclaims the works of God to the next generation (Ps. 145:4). When Moore writes that “church is special spiritual-family time,” he neglects another reality: The primary disciple-making responsibility for children in those spiritual families is given to nuclear families—namely, mothers and fathers. Modeling worship for your children is ministry. It’s a blessing for your children to watch you week after week learning from God’s Word and participating in the life of the church. It’s good to make people feel welcome at church—and that includes children. To be entrusted with children is to be entrusted with the mission of God: the passing of God’s worship from one generation to the next. Families on Mission At the same time, it’s good to be intentional about those who come into the church without a family, without community, without certainty that anyone cares about them. That’s true for our approach to lone believers, and it’s true for our approach to the lost. So how can we address that problem without treating the family like an obstacle to engaging the isolated? 1. Loving families can be welcoming families. The best path forward for engaging people alone at church isn’t by neglecting an essential commitment—the family—but by leveraging the family as a unit for mission. It’s not “Sorry kids, someone else is more important.” Instead it’s “Hey kids, this is our new friend. She’s going to sit with us today.” My wife and I have worked to show our kids not that others come before them but that others come with us because we love to include people in our lives. title: Beyond the Battlefield: Veteran Suicide and the Value of Life
summary: On Veterans Day, we celebrate the willingness of those who have served and are serving to sacrifice for our country.
content: “We’ll teach you how to kill. When you get back, you’re the VA’s problem.” That’s what they told my old team sergeant before he deployed to Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division. The risk of killing or being killed is an inescapable part of military service. In the Army, recruits go through a formation process in Basic Combat Training that turns them into soldiers. Part of this means learning that the mission always comes first, which in turn must mean they’re expendable. First aid is taught with the assumption that at some point, someone will need a tourniquet, chest seal, or body bag. After all, the enemy also learns to shoot, and sometimes the mission requires soldiers to get into harm’s way. That’s part of the tragic necessity of war. No one would have followed Washington across the Delaware or left the landing craft on D-Day if staying alive were the number-one goal. A commander’s ability to orchestrate force in combat would break down with a military unwilling to die. But this same dynamic that makes militaries potent threatens the lives of those who fight, through the tragedy of veteran suicide. Necessity of Sacrifice We must understand sacrifice as more than mere operational necessity: Something is lost when nothing is worth dying for. C. S. Lewis famously warned of the danger of making men without chests—of a people without an anchoring morality to mediate the carnal passions of the stomach and the cold calculations of the head. A society full of people consumed with their own survival doesn’t bode well for its moral character, to say nothing of its national defense. Americans ought to be thankful that thousands of young men and women regularly sign the dotted line to join the armed forces, volunteering to put their country’s well-being ahead of their own. A society full of people consumed with their own survival doesn’t bode well for its moral character. The willingness to sacrifice that makes a military effective can carry a hidden cost. What happens when a soldier learns to put his life second, then struggles to understand its value when the mission ends? A soldier who was prepared to take a bullet downrange may think little of a bottle of whiskey, a pack of cigarettes, or opening up his motorcycle on the highway. When the Mission Ends Those who make it back from combat alive aren’t entirely safe. Veterans take their own lives at roughly twice the rate of the general population. Veteran suicide stems from a number of factors, including post-traumatic stress, moral injury, difficulty transitioning to civilian life, loss of purpose and social connection, traumatic brain injury, pain, and proximity to firearms. Alongside these factors, we should consider what it means to spend years learning to put one’s life second and what happens when that lesson outlasts the mission. There’s an obvious tension when it comes to the value of life. Christians know that our lives in this world aren’t ultimate (Rev. 12:11). Christians can face death because we recognize this life’s limits, while still treating life as a gift worthy of protection. As Jesus taught, being willing to die for others is the highest form of love (John 15:13). This is why the second person of the Trinity stepped down from heaven, took on the form of a servant, and obediently followed the Father’s mission orders to death on the cross (Phil. 2:6–8). Yet Jesus didn’t throw his life away; he demonstrated perfect courage. Between the foolhardiness that leads to blood on the highway and the cowardice that keeps men in hiding when a wolf growls at the door, stands courage. As G. K. Chesterton observes, “Courage is almost a contradiction in terms. It means a strong desire to live taking the form of a readiness to die.” We see this in Christ’s agony in anticipation of the cross in the garden of Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). Yet he carried his cross anyway. Value of Life and Virtue of Sacrifice The Christian worldview ties together the value of both life and sacrifice,
author: Tommy Doles

title: How We Saw God’s Goodness Through Our Child’s Cancer
summary: It was not in the good moments where God’s care was most evident. It was in the dark moments, often at night, when we were unsure if our son would survive.
content: To encounter profound suffering is to wrestle with isolation. From Job’s seat in the ashes to your neighbor’s loss, news of suffering often includes a struggle to connect. Our family’s cancer journey was like that. We felt alone. And we sensed disconnection—even helplessness—from people who heard the news. Childhood cancer is a blessedly uncommon experience, but navigating pain is inherent to life in a fallen world. When we encounter others’ pain, we have a “Good Samaritan choice”—to step forward and show compassion or to walk away. Nightmare Our 3-year-old son, Ben, had an unexplained illness. After a week in the hospital, we were ushered into an ICU conference room full of doctors and nurses. They delivered the news: “Your son has cancer.” One of the nurses was crying before they even said a word. Our family is from Washington, DC, but we were about 10,000 miles from home. We’d been serving as missionaries in Costa Rica, yet we weren’t there either. On that January day, we were in a hospital in Sydney, Australia, on our dream trip—a family Christmas in summertime. It was quickly becoming a nightmare. The days after the diagnosis were filled with rapid changes. We couldn’t go back to Costa Rica. Returning to DC was almost impossible. The Ronald McDonald House was our new home. My daughter started kindergarten at a new school, in a new country. She drew a picture of her family. There was no home, garden, or pets—just a hospital bed. Ben on his last day of chemotherapy / Courtesy of Peter Morris Over the next six months, Ben endured 96 nights in the hospital, 25 general anesthetics, and chemotherapy so strong it could blind or even kill an adult. He was traveling through the metaphorical valley of the shadow of death, and it was decorated with bright colors and superhero stickers. May 22 is a day we still celebrate in our family as “no more chemo day.” Ben took his final dose of chemotherapy, and we rejoiced with a trip to McDonald’s and a chocolate cake. Despite the celebration, the years ahead held mortal peril. His doctor told us relapse was a risk without a treatment plan. All we could do was watch and wait. Ben was immunocompromised for the years that followed, extending into the 2020s when the disruption of a health crisis—previously rare—became globally mundane. Today, Ben’s body still carries the scars of his cancer and the side effects of the lifesaving treatment he received. But he’s a survivor. To any passerby, he looks like an ordinary 12-year-old boy. My wife and I have scars too. But we also carry the lessons the Lord taught us along the way. Those lessons are available to all believers as we encounter the pain of others. Here are three that stand out. 1. You can’t depend on people. Suffering has an odd way of resetting relationships. We saw it repeatedly, in our experience and with other cancer families we met. The apparent uniqueness of the suffering—and the emotional reactions it stirred—drove some people away. They wouldn’t, or couldn’t, step close and walk with us. However, those people stepping away opened the door to gospel opportunities for us. Australian hospitals rarely have private rooms, so we spent most of our 96 nights sharing rooms with people from diverse cultures and faiths. As other people pulled back from them, we were able to step forward and hold out the hope of the gospel in a dark and hopeless place. 2. You can depend on people. While some in our life pulled away, others chose to pull close. We were thousands of miles from our church family, but people still found ways to care for us. When we shared the news about Ben’s illness, our Facebook post reached more than 15,000 people around the world. It wasn’t the eyeballs that made a difference but the thoughtful actions. Local believers jumped into action with a meal roster. Costa Rican friends translated our English updates to equip our Spanish-speaking friends to pray. American friends prepared care packages, sent encouraging texts, and came

title: On Christmas, God Shook Up the World
summary: Advent is waiting for something that not everyone can see. Advent is preparing to receive a gift that not everyone wants.
content: Read For thus says the LORD of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of hosts. (Hag. 2:6–7) Reflect When this prophecy came to Haggai in 520 BC, did anyone imagine that God would shake up the world with a baby born to humble parents in Bethlehem? Or that “a little while” would be more than 500 years later? Yet if Advent teaches us anything, it’s that the Lord works according to his own schedule and doesn’t act as we expect. His timeline may not align with ours, but in the passage of centuries we experience his mercy. We read in 2 Peter 3:9, “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” The Lord works according to his own schedule and doesn’t act as we expect. In Hebrews 12:26, the writer expands on this relationship between patience and judgment by quoting Haggai 2. The shaking is a kind of sifting, like the sand separated from jewels in a strainer. The Lord shakes the world to sift out anyone who doesn’t worship that baby born in Bethlehem. Because even as a helpless babe, he is the King of kings and Lord of lords who will reign forever. In Jesus we see “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature,” the One who “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Heb. 1:3). One day, after a little while, that baby would grow up and exercise his power in the most unexpected way. He would submit to death, even on a cross. The day he died on Calvary, the temple curtain was torn in two. An earthquake shook the city. Rocks split at the Place of a Skull (Matt. 27:32, 51). That helpless man, bloodied and beaten, commanded more authority than anyone else had realized—including the power to judge his judges. The Roman officer who commanded 100 confessed, “Truly this was the Son of God!” (v. 54). Those who don’t follow suit will be sifted. But the shed blood of the only Son of God has the power to forgive the sins of all who repent. By this sacrifice, believers will receive a “kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Heb. 12:28). To this kingdom all the treasures of the nations will accrue, as Haggai foresaw with the temple filled by God’s glory. God did this for the Hebrews when he delivered them from slavery. They plundered the Egyptians (Ex. 12:36). And he’ll do it again when he delivers the world from death, as the kings of the earth bring their glory to the temple in the new Jerusalem (Rev. 21:24). The shed blood of the only Son of God has the power to forgive the sins of all who repent. These kings will follow a path already trod by the wise men of the east, who tracked the star to baby Jesus. From the nations they brought their treasures—gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The purported king, Herod, could only see a threat. But these wise men fell down and worshiped the baby still nursing with his mother, Mary (Matt. 2:11). Do you see the power and the glory concealed from the world while contained in that baby? Do you see in him a King whose love for sinners kept him nailed to the cross? Advent is waiting for something that not everyone can see. Advent is preparing to receive a gift that not everyone wants. Advent is enduring an unstable world with hope because an unshakable kingdom is coming—in a little while. Respond How might the Lord’s seeming lack of action express his patience for you? How could you help your non-Christian friends and family see the glory in Jesus this Advent season?
author: Collin Hansen

title: Midlife Is a Crossroads, Not a Crisis
summary: In ‘Good News for Midlife,’ Jared Wilson reminds us to embrace our midlife crossroads, find new meaning in service to others, and let this season be an opportunity to discover grace upon grace in Jesus.
content: Last year, I was sitting with an early twentysomething grad student in our church. He said he was looking for an older man to mentor him, and I started thinking through our godly, wise men in their 50s and 60s. He stopped me and clarified: He was asking me to mentor him. “Wait, you think I’m old?!” I’m 42, and to be fair, I’ve been told I’m an “old soul” my whole life. Some have wondered aloud if I was born old. While I still don’t feel old, I’ll admit this new and strange season has spurred me to go looking for wisdom. I’ll tell you, reading about midlife is depressing. According to studies, happiness in life follows a U-shaped curve. Our self-reported happiness starts high in childhood, then decreases into adolescence and further into early adulthood. It bottoms out somewhere around age 46—smack in the center of middle age—before beginning to rise again and steadily increasing into our twilight years. Further, studies have shown that depression and anxiety also are highest around the age of 45. Despite all the bad news, Good News for Midlife: Navigating Middle Age with Guts and Grace was encouraging. Writing from his early 50s, Jared Wilson, associate professor of pastoral ministry at Midwestern Baptist Theological Seminary, understands the challenges of midlife but also provides refreshing hope for those of us finding our own way through. Understand Midlife Most definitions place “middle age” as 40 to 60, but it’s probably more accurate to describe midlife in terms of its demands and responsibilities. For me, it looks something like this: I still feel energetic, but it takes far longer to recover from lost sleep, injuries, and travel. My kids are now teenagers, and some days, I only see them for a half hour. Our grocery bill is three times our first mortgage. Our parents are in their 70s and now need more support from us than we need from them. I think I’m still in touch with modern culture, but my kids assure me I’m not. I may have 40-plus years left, but it sure feels like most of my life is now behind me. Most deeply, I’m frequently reflecting on life’s disappointments and griefs, wondering if I should have done this or that differently. This is middle life. We’re too young to feel old. But we’re also too old to feel young. Wilson, who writes specifically for men entering or inhabiting these decades, acknowledges all these challenges. “But,” he writes, “while this season presents unique challenges . . . midlife also presents exciting opportunities to trust Jesus for personal, marital, and spiritual flourishing” (xi). Thankfully, Wilson helps us reframe the demands and opportunities of middle age not as a necessary crisis but as a critical crossroads . Crossroads, Not Crisis For almost 60 years, pop culture has made “midlife” nearly synonymous with “crisis.” The phrase comes from psychoanalyst Elliott Jaques’s 1965 essay “ Death and the Mid-Life Crisis ” and has been repeated across dozens of books ever since. (There’s even a board game called Mid-Life Crisis, where players aim to accumulate wealth and avoid landing on bankruptcy, divorce, and nervous breakdown.) This is middle life. We’re too young to feel old. But we’re also too old to feel young. Fortunately, recent studies suggest fewer than 20 percent of Americans experience a full-on crisis in these middle decades. Despite this, many of us face a unique temptation to flee from responsibility or forge some entirely new life. Wilson puts it poignantly: “Whether you’re in a crisis or not, at midlife you’re at a crossroads” (16). At this crossroads, we see down one path the allure of individualism and freedom from responsibility. We might simply call this path the road of empty promises. As the proverbs say, it seems right, but in the end, it leads to death (Prov. 14:12). The second path is one of embracing reality, stepping deeper into relationship, and trusting the goodness of God. This road offers no promises other than the hardships of real life. But it’s also where

title: Avoid the Trap of Bitterness
summary: Joseph avoids the trap of bitterness. And you can too, if you follow these three steps.
content: Imagine the people closest to you betray you. It’s your trust in them that lets them get close enough to hurt you so terribly. Now, imagine that this betrayal completely upends your life for years . Everything that made your life good—your family, your home, your safety—is violently taken from you. Now imagine years bleed into decades. Your life spirals into ever more pain and isolation. And every jab of hurt leads you to agonize over the initial wound: None of this would have happened if it weren’t for them. How could they do this? However, in the last few years, your fortunes have turned around. From the slums, you’re suddenly lifted to a vaulted position of power. People no longer take advantage of you but try to stay in your good graces. It doesn’t wash all the bitter memories away, but it’s something. And then, lo and behold, who happens to come before you but them . Your cruel betrayers are there, groveling, asking you for help. How would you feel? What would you do? If you haven’t picked up on it yet, this is the story of Joseph from Genesis. Sold into slavery by his brothers, Joseph walks through much injustice and suffering before being catapulted into the most powerful office in Egypt, second only to Pharaoh. And when his brothers come cringing toward him in the end, certain that Joseph will use his power to pay them back, Joseph responds with unexpected mercy, generosity, and warmth (Gen. 50:15–21) . How? Joseph avoids the trap of bitterness. And you can too, if you follow these three steps. 1. Understand Bitterness Bitterness is revealed in our emotions (coldness, anger, resentment, suspicion, revulsion), but it begins in our will. We choose bitterness when we believe that for justice or fairness to be preserved, the offender must be punished in some way. We may even claim to forgive, but in our heart of hearts, we fear that forgiveness comes at the expense of justice. So, you give your spouse the silent treatment, you cut your parents off, you make life difficult for your kids. Joseph avoids bitterness by trusting that God is the One who takes care of justice. When his brothers beg for mercy, Joseph replies, “Do not fear, for am I in the place of God?” (Gen. 50:19). Joseph knows it isn’t his place to deal out the judgment only God can give. The first step in avoiding bitterness is letting God take care of final justice (Rom. 12:14–21). Bitterness feels like a solution to the problem, but it isn’t. It’s trying to solve one sin with another sin. Which is why we’re commanded unequivocally to repent of bitterness, full stop (Eph. 4:31). We’re never told bitterness is an acceptable method to coerce repentance or pursue justice, or is permissible until the other person apologizes and makes restitution. Reconciliation requires two people who are willing. But to repent of bitterness only requires one. Bitterness feels like a solution to the problem, but it isn’t. It’s trying to solve one sin with another sin. Bitterness isn’t the path to justice—only to more bitterness. Using bitterness to pursue justice is like using a hatchet to build a house, confident it’ll work just like a hammer. 2. Unmask Bitterness We’re called to be so absolute and unqualified in rejecting bitterness because of its penchant to spread. It’s a “root” (Heb. 12:15) that will only grow and become more difficult to uproot as time goes on. Plucking up a sapling is easy; removing an oak tree isn’t. Soon, the bitterness you feel toward Person A will make you more prone to taking offense at Person B and more sensitive to Person C. Soon, you become an angry person who holds grudges. It’s a root that “defiles many.” Bitterness is hard to detect initially because it hides so effectively behind a mask of morality. The bitter person “blesses himself in his heart, saying, ‘I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart’” (Deut. 29:19). In other words, “I’m not wrong, they are! They’re the ones who hurt me!” It not only immediately puts you into a

title: Malaysian Court Sends Christian Convert’s Religious Freedom Suit to Regional Bench
summary: A 34-year-old law graduate’s multi-year battle exposes the severe reality of religious control and the legal trap facing citizens who want to leave Islam. A high-stakes constitutional challenge highlighting the erosion of religious freedom in Malaysia has taken a procedural step backward. The Kuala Lumpur High Court has ordered that a lawsuit filed by a…   The post  Malaysian Court Sends Christian Convert’s Religious Freedom Suit to Regional Bench  first appeared on  International Christian Conc
content: A 34-year-old law graduate’s multi-year battle exposes the severe reality of religious control and the legal trap facing citizens who want to leave Islam. A high-stakes constitutional challenge highlighting the erosion of religious freedom in Malaysia has taken a procedural step backward. The Kuala Lumpur High Court has ordered that a lawsuit filed by a 34-year-old legal researcher seeking legal recognition as a Christian be transferred to the Shah Alam High Court. The case lays bare the rigid and intrusive control exercised by state apparatuses and Islamic religious authorities over personal faith, showcasing a system where basic human rights — such as choosing one’s own religion — are tightly policed by the government. A Life Labeled Without Consent The plaintiff, Shameer PV, identifies as a Christian and has lived as one since he was 18. However, under strict Malaysian administrative regulations, the word “Islam” was stamped on his compulsory national identity card (MyKad) when he was just 12, following a bureaucratic policy introduced under the National Registration Act. Despite decades of personal conviction and his marriage to a Christian wife, the state continues to legally treat him as a Muslim, directly violating his parental and marital status and refusing to recognize his family. Shameer’s legal challenge names the federal government, the Selangor state government, and the Selangor Islamic Religious Council (MAIS) as defendants. He argues that labeling citizens by religion on state identity cards violates Article 11(1) of the Federal Constitution, which ostensibly guarantees every person the right to profess and practice their religion. Trapped in Shariah Bureaucracy Shameer’s ordeal underscores the labyrinthine and punishing hurdles forced upon religious minorities and converts in Malaysia’s dual-justice system, which runs a parallel set of Islamic (Shariah) courts alongside the civil judiciary. In 2018, Shameer initiated proceedings in a Selangor Shariah court seeking official recognition of his Christian faith. After an exhausting 72 court sessions spanning over seven years, the Shariah court dismissed his application in January. Rather than allowing him to move on with his life, the religious court went a step further, ordering state departments and Islamic authorities to “guide and control” his practice of Islam — effectively treating his desire to leave the faith as a disciplinary or correctional matter. Having exhausted the religious tribunal system, Shameer turned to the civil high court in July, filing an originating summons to ask the highest judicial authorities whether state-mandated religious labeling on identity cards is unconstitutional, and whether Shariah courts have any lawful jurisdiction over individuals who do not practice Islam. A Wider Crisis for Freedom of Conscience International human rights observers and religious freedom advocates have long criticized Malaysia’s legal framework regarding apostasy and conversion. While the Malaysian Constitution theoretically protects freedom of religion, civil courts have repeatedly ruled that only Islamic Shariah courts have the authority to permit someone to leave Islam — creating an effective judicial catch-22, as Shariah courts rarely grant permission to renounce the religion. For international human rights advocates and supporters of religious liberty, Shameer’s case is a stark reminder of the state-enforced religious controls facing millions in Southeast Asia. As his case moves to the Shah Alam court, the legal battle continues to test whether Malaysia’s secular constitutional framework can protect an individual’s fundamental right of conscience against a totalizing state religious bureaucracy. summary: On Nov. 1, six people took their first steps of freedom after being held by Fulani extremists for more than six months. One of them died only two days later. Bulus was one of the 11 people who were kidnapped by a Fulani militia in…   The post  Teenage Girl Dies After Six Months in Captivity  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On Nov. 1, six people took their first steps of freedom after being held by Fulani extremists for more than six months. One of them died only two days later. Hasana Bulus, 13, died in the hospital where she was taken in critical condition. Bulus was one of the 11 people who were kidnapped by a Fulani militia in April. One had escaped, but five died at the camp, and the rest were released with Bulus — including the 4-year-old daughter of a woman who had died in captivity. Bulus’ village, Awon, is predominantly Christian and has been the target of Fulani attacks, just like Ariko, a neighboring village in Kaduna state. According to a six-year study conducted by the Observatory for Religious Freedom in Africa (ORFA), Islamic Fulani militias are by far the deadliest persecutors of Christians in Nigeria. Ariko is home to the 37 Christians who were kidnapped during the Easter services earlier this year in a neighboring village. Of these, 17 people have died in captivity, 12 have escaped, and eight have since been released. The abductees from both these villages were held in the same forest hideout, where they were kept in inhumane conditions. “They [the villagers] told us how they would stay for two weeks without food,” one woman, whose father died in the camp, told Open Doors . “They only boil water to drink. That’s how they struggled before the bandits gave them corn flour, and they started making swallow (a porridge). The men are restrained, chained in groups; they are not free to move around.” All of the male abductees in these groups had died in the camp. Christian Solidarity Worldwide (CSW) is calling for Nigerian authorities to protect these communities and fight to free more people left in bondage. “We continue to urge the Nigerian government at state and federal levels to prioritize the protection of vulnerable communities throughout the nation, to combat the threat posed by the litany of terrorist groups that are active in the country far more effectively, and to secure the release of all abductees,” CSW CEO Scot Bower said. title: Al-Shabab Kills 5 Christians in Mandera, Kenya
summary: On the morning of Nov. 10, gunfire shattered the quiet along the Mandera-Arabia road in the Hagarsu area of Mandera County, Kenya. A driver and the two police reservists assigned to…   The post  Al-Shabab Kills 5 Christians in Mandera, Kenya  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On the morning of Nov. 10, gunfire shattered the quiet along the Mandera-Arabia road in the Hagarsu area of Mandera County, Kenya. Somali-based al-Shabab militants ambushed Christian construction workers inspecting a road project. The workers, who were non-locals, were targeted because of their identity and faith. A driver and the two police reservists assigned to protect them were also killed. Eight people in total were killed, with the attack following a pattern of al-Shabab-linked violence in Kenya’s northeastern borderlands. “The attack was swift but intense, leaving many traumatized, but even though we walk through the valley of the shadow of death, we will fear no evil, for Jesus is with us; His rod and staff, they comfort us,” an eyewitness said. “That’s where we draw our confidence from regardless of the present circumstances.” A Persistent Danger Mandera County lies along Kenya’s border with Somalia. For Christians living in the region, insecurity is a reality. Christians who move into the area for work are vulnerable. Churches operate under constant threat; believers travel cautiously, pastors limit evening gatherings, and congregations often worship with one eye on the door. Even traveling to work can expose Christians to danger. “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; but Jesus said, ‘I have come that they may have life, and have it to the full,’” a local church leader said. “We are becoming more vigilant and yet committed to the preaching of the gospel in the face of this constant threat from the Islamic fighters.” Always a Target Al-Shabab has repeatedly targeted Christians in the northeastern region, particularly those perceived as outsiders and those who do not share the group’s extremist religious ideology. Converts from Islam to Christianity remain especially vulnerable to intimidation, threats, and violence. The police reservists assigned to protect the workers also lost their lives. “The word of God declared that we should not grow weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up,” an eyewitness who wished to remain anonymous said. “We therefore bury the dead and comfort the widows, but we refuse to stop gathering in his name and preaching the gospel of salvation.” Responding to the killing of the five Christians, another church leader requested prayers and support for the believers in Mandera and the families of the victims. “We call upon the global church to stand with persecuted believers in Kenya and pray for the families of those killed, the wounded, and Christians across Mandera,” he said. “Pray for the protection of Christian workers, pastors, and congregations, and that they will have the courage to continue worshipping and sharing the gospel. Pray for lasting peace. The church in Mandera is not forgotten. Let us stand with them.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . title: At Least 26 Killed in DRC’s Mambasa Territory Amid Ebola Crisis
summary: Twenty-six people have reportedly been killed and several others abducted in a new attack carried out by the Islamist rebels of Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) on Nov. 10, during the night, in Mambasa territory, Ituri province, northeastern DR Congo, a country where nearly 93% of the population is Christian. According to a local association coordinator, Malikidogo, more…   The post  At Least 26 Killed in DRC’s Mambasa Territory Amid Ebola Crisis  first appeared on  International Christian Concern
content: Twenty-six people have reportedly been killed and several others abducted in a new attack carried out by the Islamist rebels of Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) on Nov. 10, during the night, in Mambasa territory, Ituri province, northeastern DR Congo, a country where nearly 93% of the population is Christian. According to a local association coordinator, Malikidogo, more than six villages were affected, including Kangwayi, Misele, Mingazi, and Mambaka. “The situation is very serious; we identified 26 people killed, several others abducted, and many families are still searching for their missing loved ones,” Malikidogo said. “Aside from the death of many people, five houses were burnt alongside some motorcycles. We are calling on the authorities to take urgent action to protect the population.” Left With Nothing Survivors who succeeded in escaping reported that many families had to run for their lives, leaving their homes and belongings behind. “We were very afraid when we realized that the enemies were already in the village when we heard people crying and others running in every direction,” one survivor said. “We just fled without having time to collect our belongings, just to save our lives. We do not know what will happen next, and we are afraid that they might come and reach Mambasa city where we are today.” The attack comes at a difficult time for local communities, which are already facing the threat of Ebola . Residents are now dealing with both the fear of the disease and the danger of further attacks. There are concerns that the violence could also make it harder to control the Ebola outbreak. People fleeing their villages may spread the disease to other communities, while insecurity could prevent health workers from reaching those who need medical help. A local leader also expressed concern about the situation and called for stronger protection of civilians. “We have suffered for many years because of the atrocities committed by ADF Islamist terrorists,” he said. “We are already struggling with Ebola, and now we are facing these attacks again. We cannot continue living like this. We are calling on the government and security forces to protect our communities before more innocent lives are lost.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: 4 Killed Days After Cantine Massacre
summary: Just days after the deadly massacre in Cantine, where at least 33 civilians were reportedly killed, suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have struck again in Beni Territory, claiming four more lives and burning several houses in Mabalako, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. At about 12:20 a.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, Mabalako once again…   The post  4 Killed Days After Cantine Massacre  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: Just days after the deadly massacre in Cantine, where at least 33 civilians were reportedly killed, suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have struck again in Beni Territory, claiming four more lives and burning several houses in Mabalako, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. At about 12:20 a.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, Mabalako once again faced ADF violence , with a fresh overnight attack in the Kamahume neighborhood. According to local civil society representatives, the death toll rose from an initial three to four, while more than seven houses were also set ablaze during the deadly incursion. The attack has renewed fears among civilians already traumatized by the violence that struck Cantine-Aloya less than a week earlier. The proximity of these two attacks in time and location has heightened concerns about the continuing threat posed by the ADF to civilian populations across Beni. “We are living in constant fear,” said Mulwahali, a survivor. “We have not yet recovered from the pain of what happened in Cantine, where innocent people were brutally killed and homes reduced to ashes. Now the violence has reached Mabalako, and once again we are mourning our loved ones and watching our homes burn. We do not know who will be next or where these attackers will strike again. We are even tired of burying our people without heads. All we want is to live in peace and sleep in our homes without fearing that we may never see another morning.” A Need for Security Local civil society representatives have appealed to security services to take full responsibility for protecting civilians, strengthen security operations, and prevent further attacks. Residents of Runzayi, Malondo, Ngazi, and Kibunamaru have also been urged to remain vigilant, maintain calm, and cooperate with security forces by reporting suspicious movements. “We cannot continue living at the mercy of armed attackers,” a local Catholic bishop said. “Although the intervention of the FARDC helped limit the destruction in Mabalako, the fact that the attackers could strike and disappear without their direction being known leaves us deeply frightened. We want security, not another massacre.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . title: The Girl They Killed for Refusing a Forced Marriage
summary: On Nov. 6, an 18-year-old Christian girl named Ajak Mabior was beaten to death in Jonglei, South Sudan, after refusing to enter a forced marriage arranged by her family. She was expected to marry an older Muslim man — a marriage she opposed because of her Christian faith and her unwillingness to be forced into it. After…   The post  The Girl They Killed for Refusing a Forced Marriage  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On Nov. 6, an 18-year-old Christian girl named Ajak Mabior was beaten to death in Jonglei, South Sudan, after refusing to enter a forced marriage arranged by her family. She was expected to marry an older Muslim man — a marriage she opposed because of her Christian faith and her unwillingness to be forced into it. After attempting to escape, she was killed by her own brother and cousin. Days later, police in Bor arrested the two men but released them without charges after family members demanded their freedom, arguing that “there was no case” because they were relatives. A Common Problem The killing has raised serious concerns among Christian leaders about the pressure Christian girls face when their faith and personal convictions conflict with family expectations. “When a young girl is killed for refusing a forced marriage, and the killers walk free because they are family, the message is clear: Tradition is stronger than the law, and stronger than the value of a life,” a local pastor said. “Many of our Christian daughters live under this same shadow.” For Christian girls in South Sudan , forced marriages can become a matter of religious persecution when they are pressured to marry outside their faith and abandon their Christian convictions. Those who refuse may face rejection, threats, intimidation, and violence from their own families. Mabior’s death highlights the vulnerability of young Christian women who seek to remain faithful to Christ while facing pressure to submit to marriages that violate their faith and conscience. “The church teaches that every life is precious because it is created in the image of God,” the pastor added. “Yet when a Christian girl refuses a marriage that would bind her against her will, she can be treated as a traitor to the community. We have buried too many who paid that price.” Seeking Justice The authorities’ response has added to the church’s concerns. Police reportedly released the suspects without the consent of the Jonglei State Caretaker Commissioner. The justification that the suspects were relatives raises serious questions about the protection available to Christian girls facing forced marriages and violence. When perpetrators are released without facing justice, vulnerable Christian women are left with little confidence that the authorities will protect their right to practice their faith and make decisions according to their conscience. “We preach freedom in Christ, but our young people still live in fear of the consequences of that freedom,” the pastor said. “If the police and local authorities remain quiet, the church becomes the only place left where these girls and boys can find a voice. We need courage to speak, and we need the wider Body of Christ to stand with us.” Mabior’s case raises concerns about forced interfaith marriages, religious pressure, and violence against young Christian women in South Sudan. “We call on the wider Body of Christ to pray for Ajak’s justice, and for the protection of Christian girls facing forced marriages because of their faith,” an International Christian Concern (ICC) staffer said. “Pray that the church will have the courage to speak against religious coercion and violence, and that the authorities will uphold the law and protect vulnerable believers.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . To support ICC’s work around the world, please give to our Where Most Needed Fund . title: Ansaru Militants Claim Killing of Muslim Cleric Who Preached Peace with Christians
summary: Ansaru militants have claimed responsibility for shooting dead a Muslim cleric known for promoting peaceful coexistence between Christians and Muslims, raising fresh concerns about the threats facing religious voices who challenge extremist ideologies in Nigeria. Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka and his friend, Adamu Abubakar, were killed Monday evening, Oct. 26, in Dutsin-Ma Local Government…   The post  Ansaru Militants Claim Killing of Muslim Cleric Who Preached Peace with Christians  first ap
content: Ansaru militants have claimed responsibility for shooting dead a Muslim cleric known for promoting peaceful coexistence between Christians and Muslims, raising fresh concerns about the threats facing religious voices who challenge extremist ideologies in Nigeria. Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka and his friend, Adamu Abubakar, were killed Monday evening, Oct. 26, in Dutsin-Ma Local Government Area of Katsina state. Two armed men riding a motorcycle reportedly opened fire on the men outside the cleric’s residence before fleeing. The Nigeria Police in Katsina confirmed the killing. The Nigerian government condemned the killings on Tuesday, while Ansaru subsequently claimed responsibility in an audio message, accusing Masussuka of being an infidel and opposing Islam. Masussuka had used social media to share Islamic teachings in Hausa, a major language spoken across northern Nigeria. In some of his videos, he called on Muslims to stop describing Christians as infidels and urged followers of both religions to live together peacefully. His message challenged religious hostility at a time when Christian communities in parts of Nigeria continue to face deadly attacks from armed extremist groups. For Christians who heard his teachings, Masussuka’s appeal for coexistence offered a reminder that resistance to religious hatred can also come from within the Muslim community. His killing has raised questions about whether those who challenge extremist interpretations of religion can safely express their views. Ansaru Accuses Cleric of Opposing Islam In an audio message released Tuesday, Oct. 27, Ansaru claimed it attacked at about 8:30 p.m. The speaker reportedly referred to Tuesday as the day of the killing, although the deaths were reported to have occurred on Monday evening. The group’s description of Masussuka as an infidel is significant because the cleric had reportedly used his platform to challenge the practice of labeling Christians in that way; the accusation against him raises concerns about the risks faced by people whose religious teachings conflict with extremist beliefs. Masussuka’s friend, Abubakar, was killed in the same shooting. Publicly available information about Abubakar’s life, his relationship with the cleric, and whether the attackers specifically targeted either man remains limited. Their deaths have left two families grieving and a community seeking answers about why the men were killed. Ansaru, formerly known as Jama’atu Ansarul Muslimina Fi Biladis Sudan, is a Nigerian jihadist organization that emerged as a breakaway faction of Boko Haram around 2012. The group has longstanding links to al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb, an al-Qaida affiliate active in the Sahel and North Africa. Ansaru has been associated with kidnappings, hostage killings, and attacks against security personnel and other targets. The United States designated the group a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2013. Ansaru is one of several armed extremist organizations operating within Nigeria’s wider security crisis. Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) have carried out attacks on Christian worshippers, churches and predominantly Christian communities, as well as killings of Muslim civilians and others they consider opponents. These groups are distinct, and responsibility for each attack must be established through evidence. Nevertheless, their activities have contributed to a climate in which religious communities fear violence, displacement and the loss of loved ones. For Nigerian Christians, the danger extends beyond individual killings. Attacks on communities, places of worship and religious leaders can disrupt church activities, force families from their homes and leave survivors struggling to rebuild their lives. title: Desperation, Fear Grow as Malaysia Clamps Down on Freedom of Conscience
summary: A wave of viral social media videos featuring Malaysian citizens publicly declaring their departure from state-sanctioned Sunni Islam has cast a harsh spotlight on the severe lack of religious freedom in the Southeast Asian nation. While state authorities have scrambled to investigate and suppress the footage, international religious freedom advocates warn that the phenomenon…   The post  Desperation, Fear Grow as Malaysia Clamps Down on Freedom of Conscience  first appeared on  International Ch
content: A wave of viral social media videos featuring Malaysian citizens publicly declaring their departure from state-sanctioned Sunni Islam has cast a harsh spotlight on the severe lack of religious freedom in the Southeast Asian nation. While state authorities have scrambled to investigate and suppress the footage, international religious freedom advocates warn that the phenomenon highlights a much deeper, systemic crisis: the complete criminalization of apostasy for ethnic Malays and the intense persecution faced by those who desire to follow other faiths, including Christianity. Under Article 160 of the Constitution of Malaysia, all ethnic Malays are legally defined as Muslims. This constitutional binding leaves no legal avenue for a Malay individual to officially change their religion. For those who experience a personal crisis of faith or choose to embrace Christianity, the path forward is fraught with state-sponsored surveillance, social ostracism, and severe legal penalties. Central to this machinery of suppression is the powerful federal agency JAKIM (Department of Islamic Development Malaysia) and state-level enforcers like JAIS (Selangor Islamic Religious Department). Together, they operate a rigid, dual-track legal system where Shariah courts hold near-absolute jurisdiction over Muslims. Requests by individuals to officially exit Islam are systematically rejected. Instead of granting freedom of conscience, JAIS and other state bodies actively weaponize mandatory detention in state-run Islamic rehabilitation centers (pusat pemurnian akidah). These centers function as forced re-education camps. Converts who are caught or who attempt to petition the courts for apostasy are routinely sentenced to months of involuntary confinement. Inside, they are subjected to intense psychological pressure, isolation, and compulsory doctrinal lectures designed to break their resolve and force a recantation. Recently, JAIS publicized a court-ordered Istitabah (forced repentance ritual) for a social media figure, signaling that the state will use its full administrative weight to enforce religious compliance. Recent landmark legal battles from 2025 and 2026 expose a devastating reality: born-Muslims face a structural wall of total rejections. In an Oct. 2, 2025 ruling, the Federal Court — Malaysia’s highest civil judiciary — completely shut down a final appeal from a 47-year-old Christian convert who spent years fighting the Shariah court system just to return to his original faith following a divorce. The apex court reaffirmed that civil courts have zero jurisdiction to override Shariah rejections, leaving the believer legally trapped. Similarly, on Jan. 6, 2025, a Selangor woman who was unilaterally converted to Islam as a child saw her final legal challenge collapse at the Federal Court, cementing the precedent that her state identity card (MyKad) must permanently brand her as a Muslim. Even elderly believers who have secretly practiced their faith for decades are being hunted through bureaucracy. In June 2026, a 58-year-old mother filed a prominent judicial review against the National Registration Department (JPN) after they flatly refused to remove the “Islam” label from her identification card — despite her having formally converted out of Islam via a deed poll more than 30 years ago. JPN continues to trap her under state custody, demanding a clearance letter from the Shariah court that officials refuse to grant. The statistics highlight how tightly the trap is wound. Historical data shows that out of 863 formal applications submitted nationwide to leave Islam during a 10-year period, only 168 were granted. Legal analysts emphasize that nearly 100% of those rare exceptions were administrative clerical corrections in East Malaysia — such as a Jan. 7 Kota Kinabalu High Court ruling where a father and three children successfully proved they were raised Christian and that an NRD officer had made a data-entry error. title: More than 30 Killed in Latest ADF Attack
summary: Fear, bloodshed, and devastation have once again descended upon communities in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) stormed Cantine in the Madiwe sector of Beni territory, in the North Kivu Province during the night of Thursday, Nov. 5, into the early hours of Nov. 6, leaving civilians dead, homes…   The post  More than 30 Killed in Latest ADF Attack  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: Fear, bloodshed, and devastation have once again descended upon communities in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) stormed Cantine in the Madiwe sector of Beni territory, in the North Kivu Province during the night of Thursday, Nov. 5, into the early hours of Nov. 6, leaving civilians dead, homes burning, and an already vulnerable population gripped by terror. Justin Paluku, president of the Civil Society Forces Vives of Madiwe, confirmed that the provisional death toll stood at more than 30 civilians. “For families that went to bed hoping to wake up to another ordinary morning, the night turned into a nightmare of unimaginable suffering,” Paluku said. “We are deeply concerned about the safety of our population. Christian Civilians cannot continue living like prisoners in their own communities, constantly wondering when armed men will strike again. Our people deserve protection, peace and the freedom to live without fear.” Seeking Safety As news of the attack spread, residents began fleeing Cantine toward neighboring areas considered relatively safer. Children, women, and the elderly are among those facing the uncertainty of displacement, leaving behind homes, livelihoods, and personal belongings. For Christian survivors, the immediate concern is no longer what tomorrow will bring, but whether they will survive another attack . “We heard the sounds of violence, and fear immediately took control of us,” a survivor of the attack said. “We had no time to collect our belongings. All we wanted was to escape with our lives. We have lost our sense of security, and we do not know whether we will ever return to our homes again.” The reported burning of homes and looting of property represent more than material destruction. They strip Christian families of their dignity, deepen their vulnerability, and leave children exposed to hunger, insecurity, and psychological trauma. The wider Beni region has endured years of repeated attacks, killings, abductions, and displacement attributed to armed groups, particularly the ADF. Each new incident adds another painful chapter to the suffering of communities that continue to demand protection and justice. To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: The Journey Through Persecution to Graduation
summary: On Nov. 6, Titus Hassan Malika stood with his classmates and received his diploma — a quiet but powerful moment marking the end of a long, difficult road. The Sudanese Christian, who fled violence and persecution in his homeland, had received support from International Christian Concern (ICC). With God’s help, what once seemed impossible had become reality. …   The post  The Journey Through Persecution to Graduation   first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On Nov. 6, Titus Hassan Malika stood with his classmates and received his diploma — a quiet but powerful moment marking the end of a long, difficult road. The Sudanese Christian, who fled violence and persecution in his homeland, had received support from International Christian Concern (ICC). With God’s help, what once seemed impossible had become reality. “The support I received from ICC is a dream come true,” Malika said. “I never imagined that someone would stand with me for so many years, believing in my future when I could barely see it myself. This graduation is not only my achievement — it is the fruit of their faithfulness and God’s provision.” Titus grew up in Sudan, where following Jesus grew increasingly dangerous . As pressure on Christian communities intensified amid conflict and targeted hostility, he was forced to leave everything behind. With little more than his faith, he crossed into Kenya as a refugee, carrying the weight of loss, uncertainty, and the hope that God still had a future for him. By His Side In 2023, ICC stepped into that uncertainty. Through consistent support, practical help, encouragement, and the means to continue his studies, we walked with Titus through years of hardship. The path was not easy. He faced the daily challenges of life, the lingering trauma of persecution, and the enduring discipline of education while far from home. Yet he pressed on. “Jesus Christ has been the center of my life from the day I fled Sudan until this moment,” he said. “When I had no home, he was my shelter. When fear tried to silence me, he gave me courage. Every step of this journey has been possible only because he walked with me and never left me alone.” As he steps into his next chapter, Titus carries both a Bachelor’s degree in business administration and management, as well as a testimony that God can bring beauty from ashes, and that the Body of Christ, when it stands with the persecuted, can help rewrite a life marked by suffering into one marked by grace. “I give thanks to God for ICC, for they have been the hands and feet of Christ to me,” he said. “As it is written, ‘And my God will meet all your needs according to the riches of his glory in Christ Jesus’ (Philippians 4:19). Truly, the Lord has done this. May he continue to bless those who have poured out their lives so that I could stand here today.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . To support ICC’s work around the world, please give to our Where Most Needed Fund . content: Psalm 111:2 is one of my favorite verses in the Bible: Great are the works of the L ORD , studied by all who delight in them. Derek Kidner calls these lines “God’s charter for the scientist and artist” ( Psalms 73–150 , 432). But the scope of this charter extends far beyond the laboratory and the studio. It is the liberating banner that flies over all of Christian education. A manifesto for holy curiosity. A sovereign call to attention. Throughout Psalm 111, the anonymous author bends all his poetic effort to awaken us to the works of God so we might be alive to the God who works. He wants to pry our eyelids open with the crowbar of poetry so we might behold what God does and tremble in awe of him. He’s cleaning our lenses so that God’s works explode with clarity and color, kindling our curiosity and inspiring us to attend and adore. Doesn’t that sound wonderful? Don’t you ache to be quite awake, rather than asleep? Don’t you long to live with your eyes wide open to God and his works? If so, consider three questions Psalm 111 raises about why studying God’s works delights us. Back to School First, what does it mean to study God’s works? The word “study” ( dāraš ) means “to seek out, to experience, to attend to.” Its scope defies the confines of ivory towers or professional scholarship. The poet’s main thrust in this psalm is for you , dear reader, to study diligently in the schoolhouse of God’s works. Psalm 111:2 exhorts us to practice omnivorous attentiveness . Omnivorous describes someone who devours without discrimination, like a hungry teenager ransacking a full fridge. Those who practice omnivorous attentiveness , then, are awake to everything God does; they gobble up all his works, both the big and the small, the miraculous and the mundane. The constant exclamation of omnivorous attentiveness is “Wow, Lord, look at that !” It is the exact opposite of taking anything for granted. Those who cultivate this kind of attention live with their eyes wide open. They are awake. Wondrous Works of God But awake to what, exactly? What does Psalm 111 teach us about the scope of God’s works? The word for “works” in verse 2 means acts or creations. The term wraps its arms around all God does and says, all the fruit of his omnipotent labor. If we look at Psalm 111 as a whole, the poet leaves God’s works deliciously ambiguous. His deliverance of Israel in the exodus colors the background of this psalm, but the references are vague — intentionally so. By avoiding specifics and gesturing broadly at the wondrous works of God, our poet throws the doors wide open to omnivorous attention. He invites us to step into the entire theater of creation and redemption and marvel at the Director who runs the show. He excludes nothing from our eyes-wide-open study. Let’s follow our poet’s lead and take a brief tour through some of God’s works in this poem. General and Special Revelation To begin, verse 7 points to God’s general revelation : “The works of his hands are faithful and just.” In the Psalms, “the works of his hands” most often refers to God’s works of creation. Like an art connoisseur, our poet beckons us into the vast gallery of God’s glory to stop and admire the wonders within. Consider one example: trees. God loves trees; both his book and world are crowded with them. And no wonder! These magnificent creatures take a clear liquid, an invisible gas, and sunlight, and then — by green magic that remains a mystery to most of us — transform those ingredients into the largest, hardest, oldest living things on earth. Trees are star-powered wood towers. And time would fail to tell of children’s smiles and summer storms, eggs and honeybees, sunrises and starscapes, the extravagant green of grass and the large, slow oddity of cows. Indeed, great are the works of God! But the second half of verse 7 also highlights the privilege of God’s special revelation : “All his precepts are trustworthy.” The works of God include the words of God . General revelat
