title: First Person: The Great Commission — Our Master’s Moon Shot
summary: I was born in 1961. The U.S. president at that time was John F. Kennedy. In that year he issued a challenge to our nation. It was that we build a rocket ship, put men in it, send it to the moon, have them walk on the surface, plant our flag, then return them safely to earth. He called on the nation to accomplish this within a decade. This extraordinary, demanding, costly endeavor is known to history as Kennedy’s “moon shot.” The nation rose to the challenge. I still remember watching in 1969 a g
content: Jeff Ginn, IMB's senior ambassador for U.S. and global relations, speaks to a crowd gathered to discover new ways to partner in God's mission. Ginn is available to speak in churches on behalf of the IMB. IMB Photo Portrait of Jeff Ginn, IMB senior ambassador of U.S. and global relations. IMB Photo I was born in 1961. The U.S. president at that time was John F. Kennedy. In that year he issued a challenge to our nation. It was that we build a rocket ship, put men in it, send it to the moon, have them walk on the surface, plant our flag, then return them safely to earth. He called on the nation to accomplish this within a decade. This extraordinary, demanding, costly endeavor is known to history as Kennedy’s “moon shot.” The nation rose to the challenge. I still remember watching in 1969 a grainy, black-and-white broadcast as Neil Armstrong stepped on the surface of the moon and declared, “One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” We often think of the astronauts with admiration. And rightly so. They were courageous. However, let’s note that the Apollo mission employed some 400,000 additional people to fulfill the mission. Team members included mission controllers, metal fabricators, communication specialists, caterers, engineers, scientists, nurses, doctors, mathematicians and computer programmers. Beyond these, all U.S. taxpayers contributed! It took a nation to get two astronauts to the moon and safely return them! That term, “moon shot,” has made its way into our vocabulary. It can be used for other daring, costly, and valuable undertakings. It is fair, then, to say that the Lord Jesus, our Master, has a moon shot of His own! His mission merits our lives and resources. His mission includes all who name Christ as Lord collaborating to fulfill it. At the International Mission Board, all our plans, strategies and decisions center around this biblical idea that we all must work together to fulfill Christ’s mission. We all must pray. We all must give. We all must go. We all must send. Matthew 28:18-20 is one passage, perhaps the best known, that gives us the details for our mission. The name that evangelicalism has given to this passage is “The Great Commission.” The word “commission” is not one that we use commonly. It simply means a command. How interesting that, with hundreds of commands in Scripture, this is this one that gets the definitive article, “the,” and the adjective, “great.” Does it merit that moniker? I say that it does, and I offer three reasons why. Because it makes a great claim When quoting the Great Commission, it is common for folks to omit verse 18 and simply begin with verse 19. But to do so undercuts the weight that Jesus’ claim in verse 18 adds. There He claims to have all authority in heaven and on earth. That essentially is a claim to divinity — to supremacy. He is saying that He is the King above all kings and the Lord above all lords. When we consider His claim, we all have a choice to make. To borrow from C. S. Lewis, we could decide that He is a liar or a lunatic. Following liberal theologians or Muslim theology, we could decide that much of what is taught about Him in the New Testament is the stuff of legend — that the disciples exaggerated and “created” the Christ of faith. Jeff and Nell Ginn served with the International Mission Board in Colombia. Jeff currently serves churches as IMB senior ambassador. IMB Photo But the decision that I have made (and on which I’ve staked my eternal destiny) is that He is not a liar, nor a lunatic, nor a legend. He is, in fact, Lord! My prayer is that all will decide similarly. As such, He has the authority to issue any commission and our only right response is, “Yes, Lord!” His authority is why, 35 years ago, my wife, Nell, and I said “yes” when He called us to serve with the IMB in Cali, Colombia.  It was under His authority that we planted churches and taught future leaders in the seminary there. Because it gives a great command Not only is it the Gr

title: IMB seeks teachers, healthcare workers, business professionals to serve as missionaries
summary: When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. IMB leaders report that critical roles such as teachers, healthcare workers, counselors, accountants, logistics specialists and member care personnel are helping advance the Great Commission in ways many churches never see. Doreen Baker, IMB director
content: IMB missionary Dr. Heidi Haun, left, checks on patients at Baptist Medical Centre in Nalerigu, Ghana. There are needed roles for IMB missionaries in healthcare, ministering to the needs of local populations and utilizing this time to minister to spiritual needs. IMB Photo When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. IMB leaders report that critical roles such as teachers, healthcare workers, counselors, accountants, logistics specialists and member care personnel are helping advance the Great Commission in ways many churches never see. Doreen Baker, IMB director of TCK (third culture kid or missionary kid) education, sees a constant need for education professionals. Teachers are needed in international schools, which cover a variety of global educational entities, and in other settings to provide for missionary kids and their educational needs. “Teachers are significant in that not only are they providing instruction for students, but they are an integral part of the core missionary task ,” Baker said. “We also have great needs for consultants to support our families on the field with their children’s education in many ways.” Baker previously served 25 years teaching in Asia and experienced how education creates access to missions where traditional pathways may be limited. IMB missionary Ellie Bohrer teaches a 12th grade World Views class at Black Forest Academy in Germany. The IMB is seeking other educators, like Bohrer, who are willing to use their skills on the mission field. IMB Photo Scott Ray, IMB senior director of global deployment, noted that many missionary positions go unfilled simply because they fall outside traditional perceptions of missionary service. He said professional skills can provide both practical ministry support and access to countries where traditional missionary visas are difficult to obtain. Opportunities exist for finance professionals, veterinarians, medical workers, Send Relief personnel and others. Healthcare remains one of the most strategic areas in demand. Tom Hicks, IMB director of global health strategies, said many medical professionals have the wrong perception about mission work. “We do have an issue where people will select out because they don’t think that what they do is useful on the mission field,” he said. In reality, Hicks said many areas across the globe are increasingly seeking family medicine physicians, internists, pediatricians, pediatric nurse practitioners, OB providers, physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech pathologists and lactation consultants. The need is especially significant in sub-Saharan Africa, where young populations create a growing demand for pediatric care. Healthcare professionals also provide a unique advantage in countries that restrict missionary activity. “Missionaries with a vocational value, like healthcare missionaries, have opportunities to go places that others can’t go,” Hicks said. Another often-overlooked ministry is member care, which focuses on the spiritual, emotional, mental and relational health of IMB missionaries. Chris Martin is the IMB director of global member care. “Member care missionaries stand alongside those missionaries that are thought of traditionally as church planters or evangelists and support them,” Martin said. Many who serve in these roles come from counseling backgrounds and help missionaries navigate stress, conflict, grief and other challenges that can affect long-term ministry effectiveness. Martin compares their role to Aaron and Hur in Exodus 19, holding up Moses’ arms during battle, strengthening those serving on the front lines. IMB missionary Glen Garner uses his business skills and experience as the logistics director for missionaries serving globally. He lives in Lima, Peru, with his wife, Shannon
author: Chris Doyle

title: IMB missionary sees God at work through new believer and local church

They went to the park to share the gospel, but approaching a man in their Muslim-majority city was out of the question. They kept walking and watching. content: In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo Twenty minutes had passed already. The sun was going down, and they were looking everywhere, but they only saw men in the park. Sophia, an International Mission Board missionary, joined another IMB missionary and Maryam, a South Asian Christian. They went to the park to share the gospel, but approaching a man in their Muslim-majority city was out of the question. They kept walking and watching. Even if they went home without a single conversation, Sophia knew Maryam would want to try again. This woman who had grown up with a distrust of Muslims, now searched a park for a Muslim woman to tell about Jesus. When Sophia first invited her along, Maryam never imagined a Muslim could come to know Jesus. But the more they went out sharing the gospel together, the more God softened her heart. “One day, I found she was sharing in the park by herself, without me,” Sophia said with a laugh. These days, she shares regularly — with classmates, with rickshaw drivers, with women in the park, when she can find them. God transformed Maryam’s heart. He could transform this walk through the park, too. “So we stopped,” Sophia said, “and prayed, ‘God, give us just one woman to talk to.’” Then they spotted her — a girl sitting alone on a bench. Meeting the girl on the bench She looked like other conservative Muslim women in the area, covered in black except for her face. They approached casually, not wanting to frighten her. It was Eid al-Adha – “one of the biggest Muslim holidays here,” Sophia said. They greeted her and asked about her holiday plans. Her name was Tara, and she wasn’t intimidated at all. “You may think I’m a Muslim from the way I dress,” she said, “but actually in my heart, I have left Islam.” “I was a little shocked,” Sophia said, hearing such a bold statement from a stranger. Tara told them she was a university student at a conservative Islamic school, but she had grown disillusioned and discontent with the religion. “ I don’t believe in Islam anymore,” Tara said. Without knowledge of God, she had no one to pray to, and it left her lonely. She’d been searching — Buddhism and Hinduism from friends, even a meeting with atheists, who struck her as unhappy, following only themselves. “Do you know any Christians?” Sophia asked. “Would you like to hear what we believe?” “Sure, please share.” They read about Jesus’ birth, and Tara was hungry for more. When she asked about church, Sophia described their congregation of about 40 believers, many from a Muslim background. Though she wasn’t ready to visit the church, Tara continued her interest in learning. Sophia and Maryam met with her every week in coffee shops, tea shops, Sophia’s home, wherever they could talkthat wasn’t too loud or have “too many ears and eyes” observing them. Finding her closest friend They read through the Gospel of John. One November day in a coffee shop, they reached the passage on the Samaritan woman at the well, and Sophia noticed Tara was crying. “Tara, I see you have tears,” Sophia said. “Let’s stop. Let’s talk about it .” That day, Tara prayed to receive Christ. Soon after, she wanted to visit the church, though nervous how believers would receive her in a hijab. “They will love you,” Sophia told her. “Don’t worry.” Tara went and was welcomed. That Christmas, 80 people packed Sophia’s apartment, singing and dancing in circles. Across the room, Sophia saw Tara, wearing red Christmas garland like a scarf and a smile stretched across her face. “Tara grew up very conservative – music was not even allowed in her home. But now she’s dancing, worshiping the Lord with us with music and songs.” In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo That spring, Tara was baptized.
author: Emily Hall

title: God remains faithful through IMB missionaries in Italy

And the meaning is different for them than it is for the thousands who travel there to visit that site. “If you come to Rome, you can come to a place called the Holy Steps,” Jason said. “People go there, and they’ll crawl up on their knees and pray the rosary all the way up.” From the top of the steps, a mural depicting Jesus on the Cross looks down on those making the pilgrimage. For Jason and Lizzy, it’s a spiritu
content: The eastern face of St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican City in Rome, Italy, is famous for its central balcony from which popes give their papal addresses. Most people in Rome have at least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” IMB Photo In the city where Jason and Lizzy Davis serve, some steps have a lot of meaning. And the meaning is different for them than it is for the thousands who travel there to visit that site. “If you come to Rome, you can come to a place called the Holy Steps,” Jason said. “People go there, and they’ll crawl up on their knees and pray the rosary all the way up.” From the top of the steps, a mural depicting Jesus on the Cross looks down on those making the pilgrimage. For Jason and Lizzy, it’s a spiritual experience, a picture of a religion that asks people to earn their way to Jesus. “That’s really the opposite of what the gospel is. The gospel is Jesus saying, ‘No, you can’t do it . . . no matter how good you think you are,’” they said. Most people in Rome have at the very least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism, as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” Jason explained, “It’s where the Pope lives in the Vatican. It’s very much part of the religion and culture. It’s all intertwined here.” An ‘unavoidable’ call Jason and Lizzy are investing their lives as International Mission Board missionaries in Rome, Italy, to share the truth of the gospel. The Davises partner with national believers through a new church plant, and they’re seeking to plant more churches within the city. Lizzy said for her, the call to missions was unavoidable. “I grew up as a third culture kid, or a missionary kid. My parents were on the mission field, as were my grandparents, all with the International Mission Board.” Then her family moved to Virginia for her dad to work for IMB’s home office staff. As a middle schooler and high schooler, every time Lizzy heard about the need for the gospel to go forth, she felt a burden, a “burning” in her heart. She didn’t know what God would do with that, but she had a feeling she would see one day. Now, years later, she and Jason spend their time trying to find as many opportunities as they can to invite people into their home so they can share the hope of Jesus with them. That can mean Bible study or simply sharing a meal. ‘Completely lost’ Jason has been surprised by just how often people are willing to talk about faith. “You can get into spiritual conversations very quickly with people, especially if you’re just open and honest with them.” Lizzy shared that one of the easiest ways to do this is to be willing to let your day be interrupted. “That’s something I’ve seen Jason do firsthand in our neighborhood. He walks down the street, and everybody knows him because he stops and takes the time to ask them questions about their families, gets to know people, gets to know the newspaper stand guy and the guy at the fruit stand and the grocery store ladies.” She emphasized that caring about people is “what Christ would do.” The Davises, whose previous mission service prevents their photos from being published, live in a neighborhood of about 130,000 people. Their church of 15 people is the only evangelical congregation there. Lizzy said the area is “truly a lost, completely lost, dark neighborhood” with people who have never heard the gospel. Thousands more come to their area on a religious quest. The Davis family’s neighborhood is home to the Basilica Papale di San Paolo (the Papal Basilica of Saint Paul), one of the city’s four major basilicas. “So we get a lot of people coming on spiritual journeys, visiting our neighborhood, seeking some sort of spiritual experience. And oftentimes it’s just trying to earn their salvation,” she added. Jason described this environment as “a genuine need for people to actually hear the gospel and know that their sins can be forgiven and they can have an assurance of that.” IMB missionaries Jason and Liz

title: Global missionary partners expand gospel work through IMB teams
summary: Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. The percentage of evangelical Christians in the Azores and Japan is similar, with both populations under 1%. Couto is a fourth-generation Christian, a rarity on the small islands. content: Rebeca Couto, a global missionary partner from the Azores islands, practices writing characters with her tutor in Japan. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto poses with her violin. Couto is a professional violinist who is serving as a global missionary partner with the IMB in Japan. Doors have opened for her to use her skills with evangel ical Japanese musicians who perform. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. The percentage of evangelical Christians in the Azores and Japan is similar, with both populations under 1%. Couto is a fourth-generation Christian, a rarity on the small islands. She is one of few, if any, believers in the Azores with such a long spiritual lineage. This rich legacy shaped her and prepared her for ministry. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ to be missionaries, wherever they are, whatever they’re doing, and whatever God has equipped them with,” Couto said. Couto’s great-grandfather became a Christian through the witness of missionaries from the United Kingdom. Later, missionaries from the Foreign Mission Board, now the International Mission Board, started the first Baptist work in the Azores by planting an English-speaking church near an American military base. A Baptist Brazilian couple planted a Portuguese-speaking church, which became the congregation where Couto grew up and was commissioned as a missionary. Ministry has been passed down through the generations of her family. Couto’s father has pastored for 20 years, and both of her parents have been involved in ministry for most of their lives. Couto now serves in Japan as a global missionary partner, a missionary who is financially supported by a sending church or organization in their home country and serves with IMB teams. Close to 400 GMPs currently serve on IMB teams around the world. Language learning Couto is immersed in language study in Yokohama, Japan. She had a head start before she even arrived. After graduating from high school, Couto moved from the Azores to Lisbon to pursue a degree in music. She spent hours on public transportation and wanted a challenge to pass the time. She decided to study Japanese because she thought it sounded beautiful. At the time, she had no intention of becoming a missionary in the traditional sense. However, the more she learned about the language and the culture, her burden for the lost grew. She began researching Christianity in Japan. “I understood how bleak the scenario was, and how much the country needed Jesus. I struggled with that calling because the doors were closed, and it didn’t seem possible to come to Japan for a myriad of reasons,” Couto said. After finishing master’s degrees in music and violin performance, along with a seminary degree, Couto was considering pursuing a Ph.D. or returning to seminary when her seminary professors, IMB missionaries Jonathan and Bethany Sharp, contacted her about serving as a missionary in Japan. They introduced her to the GMP program and invited her to attend a missions immersion school they piloted . Music to their ears As a professional violinist, Couto brought her violin to Japan, unsure of what opportunities existed, but she knew her call to the mission field somehow involved her gifting. “I see myself as having been called to serve through music. I never even conceived doing missions while excluding the violin entirely,” Couto said. She continued, “Music is such a universal way to connect with people, and it’s so intuitive to pair that with the gospel and with God’s message to people’s hearts.” While she knew the Lord would somehow open a door for her to use the violin for kingdom work, she was at peace with the possibility that, for a season, she may not be as active in music. That, however, was not the case. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ

title: IMB missionaries use home, cafes, apps to open doors for gospel conversations in Spain
summary: Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise w
content: Men and women gather to discuss spiritual topics with Caleb and Carina Beaty, International Mission Board missionaries who serve in Madrid. IMB Photo Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise when they arrive. Caleb said he always has a list of questions that begin broadly and funnel into questions such as, “If there were a God …” or “What do you think Christians believe about that?” or “Why do you think religions have such different perspectives?” The Beatys’ goal in these conversations is to work toward deeper worldview questions within 45 minutes to an hour. Most of the people who attend their Meetup group are from Madrid, but they also have conversations with people from other countries. During one Meetup, Caleb and Carina shared how creation was perfect, but sin led to a world separated from the Father. God offers salvation through the death and resurrection of Jesus, they explained. “There are times we’re able to get to a clear gospel presentation with a group of people, and sometimes we’re doing pre-evangelism.” Caleb said. Some repeat attendees who have been attending for more than a year quickly jump to the heart of the discussion. “All right, Caleb, what’s the Bible say about suffering?” they’ll ask. Caleb and Carina then have the opportunity to share the Christian perspective. IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty and their children pose for a photo in a park in Madrid, Spain.  IMB Photo Spain has secularized rapidly since the 1990s, Caleb said. While many may think of it as a Catholic nation, many people do not know the basic tenets of Christianity. “We’ve got all the churches, we’ve got the cathedrals, and they do processions, but the average person on the street does not know anything about the gospel and does not know anything about Jesus,” Caleb said. Younger Spaniards are drawn to their group and are receptive to the gospel because they don’t have a spiritual foundation or know anyone who does. “There’s just this curiosity because, for a lot of them, they’ve never met someone who actually believes that God exists, and that changes your life,” Carina said. “I’ve had people completely shocked that we believe in God. ‘You really believe that God exists?’ They can’t wrap their mind around that.” During one Meetup, a man contrasted Protestant and Catholic beliefs by saying Protestants focus on Jesus’ suffering and Catholics on Mary’s grief. Caleb responded that evangelicals focus on the resurrection. When Caleb said Jesus rose from the dead, the man replied that he needed to look into that. Caleb said encounters like that reveal how little many Spaniards know about the gospel. Caleb noted the irony of the man’s sharing the Catholic perspective without truly understanding it. He is not the only person the Beatys have met who has missed the heart of the gospel. A friend of the Beatys told them she’d heard Jesus died, but she hadn’t heard he rose from the dead. A man reads a passage of Scripture during a Bible study hosted by IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty at their family’s apartment in Madrid, Spain. Five atheists began attending their Bible study after attending the couple’s Meetup group. IMB Photo The Beatys also host seasonal outreach events through the Meetup. Members from their church in Madrid have started attending the Meetup to learn how the Beatys lead discussions. Their group has become so popular, a waitlist has formed. Caleb and Carina host a small-group Bible study in their home. Five atheists who joined their Meetup now attend the Bible study.
author: Tessa Sanchez

title: AAEO, LMCO totals signal Southern Baptist support for, focus on Great Commission
summary: NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion
content: IMB Graphic NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. For some it is a few hundred dollars, for others several thousand.” The Annie Armstrong offering supports more than 3,000 missionaries in North America, including the ongoing work of church planting in the U.S. and Canada. In 2025, Southern Baptists planted the largest number of churches, 699, since 2016. Including church plants and replants, Southern Baptists have surpassed 700 new churches in four of the last five years. More than 12,000 churches have been planted since 2010. To go along with the increased giving totals to the SBC’s missions offerings, Southern Baptists have also increased their local outreach efforts, indicating that the focus is not just on giving but on sending. Baptism totals have increased in each of the last five years, recovering from the pandemic-year low in 2020 to surpass the 2017 total. The five consecutive years of increase marked the first such streak in approximately 75 years. To Jordan Adams, unheard of things like 38 baptisms in one worship service have become “heard of” for his congregation. Several years ago, Adams planted a church in West Lafayette, Indiana, to reach students at Purdue University. “Now,” he says, “we’re seeing a movement of the gospel that I’m convince

title: Oklahoma Baptists join Sending Church Lab to strengthen missionary support
summary: The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning ce
content: Staff members at First Baptist Church in Wagoner, Oklahoma, evaluate their church’s involvement with missions and missionary support. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. For IMB missionaries Peter and Katie Weeks, that clarity is especially valuable. They participated in the lab alongside church leaders. Their real names have been changed to protect their work in Southeast Asia. “There’s no other place I’d rather be during these few days than here,” Peter said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. From a missionary perspective, she believes the lab addresses a common challenge. “It’s hard to know sometimes as churches how to be a good sending church and how to support missionaries,” she sa

title: Digital doors open the gospel for islanders in Southeast Asia
summary: Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian isl
content: Just as young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than in person, the same is true for people in Southeast Asia. IMB missionaries are creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content to connect with the lost through the internet. IMB Photo Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian islands are harder to accomplish. While teams travel to these remote islands often, living in a sparsely populated, animistic background culture as a foreigner creates suspicion and make long-term ministry difficult. Furthermore, young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than they are in person, Clarkston said, which is true of the islanders as well. Attempting to have a spiritual conversation face-to-face has become “too much” for locals, Clarkston shared. So, how do you share the gospel with multiple people groups who are constantly online and less comfortable with in-person interactions? For these Southeast Asia teams, digital engagement — the use of social media platforms to share a message — has become a plausible and effective entry point. The social media agency We Are Social confirmed this, revealing that 82.4% of Southeast Asia’s population uses the internet. “No matter where they go, how far they go, how remote it is, people have phones,” Clarkston and her team realized, “And though sometimes they do have to climb up the highest peak to get reception, people do it.” Clarkston’s team has begun creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content in hopes of building bridges to the islanders through the internet. Viewers can click on the ad to message back and forth with a responder, a local believer or missionary who is available to pray, build relationships and answer spiritual questions. “It seems like locals are more open to watching those things in the privacy of their own cell phones,” Clarkston said. Clarkston intends to use digital engagement as a means for initial contact with people with animistic backgrounds, evangelism and, eventually, discipleship. She said that this new ministry has the potential to open doors with individuals across these islands who would normally never reach out on their own or respond to the gospel in person. “Maybe they’ll respond this way,” Clarkston said, “I know without a shadow of a doubt that God is calling people to Himself.” Now, more than ever, technology has a grip on society. Many spend hours each day mindlessly scrolling, searching for meaning, for happiness. And now, more than ever, there is an incredible opportunity to plant seeds across Southeast Asian islands through digital engagement. The IMB Southeast Asia team gives praise to the Lord that He has provided a creative way to reach the lost and plant seeds. Pray the people among the Southeast Asian islands would see these ads and engage with responders boldly, even though they may face persecution or harm because of it. Names were changed for security. Mikah Young is serving overseas with the IMB. The work of the IMB is sustained through faithful giving to the Cooperative Program and the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering ® . title: IMB missionaries share vision for Seoul during Serve Tour
summary: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technol
content: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technology, K-cosmetics. Yes, good things… But many Korean people are struggling right now.” The Sols, who were featured in the 2025 Week of Prayer for International Missions , continue to rely on the prayers of faithful Southern Baptists. Prayers sustain them and help to push back the darkness they confront in their home culture. Hun often describes that hidden struggle with a Korean word: han. There is no simple English translation. It speaks to a deep sorrow shaped by generations of war, division, loss, and the quiet resolve to endure. Hun sees it in the young adults he meets every week—people navigating loneliness and relentless expectations, quietly asking what their lives are for beneath a veneer of success. Han is heavy. For many young adults, that weight can feel unbearable. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among teenagers and young adults in South Korean. Hun and Eunjoo see the effects of that reality every day, and it’s one reason they believe they have no time to waste. That understanding shaped the week of Serve Tour Seoul this summer. There were no construction sites, no paintbrushes, no tools or work gloves. Instead, the team stepped into ministries local churches had been faithfully building long before the volunteers arrived. In May, 27 volunteers from seven churches across the United States came alongside local churches already serving their communities in Seoul, Paju, and Gwangju. They taught English classes, ran children’s camps, walked neighborhoods in prayer, distributed food, and sat down with college students, one conversation at a time. For Nick Holst of Sandals Church in Riverside, California, the goal was simple enough to say in a sentence: “We came to meet people,” Holst said. “We want to hear their stories, and that leads to some very meaningful connections as you get past the surface into something deeper.” That’s where the week actually lived: past the surface and past the small talk, where the quiet weight of han is often carried without words. On college campuses, volunteers played games, asked questions and mostly just listened. Some conversations lasted a few minutes and ended there. Others kept going long past the point where either person expected them to. One morning, after asking his church back home to pray, Holst sat down with a university student named Intec. They talked about culture first, the way strangers do, and then the conversation turned somewhere neither of them planned. “I got to ask him, ‘What do Koreans believe?’” Holst recalled. Intec said he didn’t believe in God. Then he recited John 3:16 from memory, word for word, a verse he’d heard somewhere along the way and never forgotten. Before they parted, Holst asked if he could pray that God would keep drawing Intec toward Himself. “He said yes.” In a city where many conversations never move beyond the surface, the exchange was a reminder of why the team had come. Not to win an argument, but to listen, to ask questions, and to trust God with what happens next. The same pattern unfolded elsewhere, beginning in classrooms and ending on city streets. Jeremy Doyle, missions pastor at Valley Baptist Church in Bakersfield, California, watched an English conversation club grow from two students on its first night to eight by the second. Nobody advertised it as anything more than a place to practice English, but the room kept filling, and so did the conversations. The team’s work with students didn’t stop there. title: Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Ken and Sally discovered a way to give God’s Word — a gift they’d had access to their whole lives — to others.    The post  Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: What did your journey to faith look like? Perhaps it was a story of how God showed up in the midst of uncertainty, doubt or fears. Maybe it involved Him seeking you out and rescuing you. Or maybe you grew up in a Christian household and your story is a bit different — perhaps your family regularly read the Bible together and have always known about Jesus’ love. Ken Trager was raised that way. He reflected, “I think when you’re raised in a Christian home … and you have the routines of a life that is built around church and prayer, you just take it for granted.” He added, “It was just the air I breathed.” For Ken and his wife, Sally, faith was always part of their stories. They were each raised in Christian homes, followed Christ, got baptized and had parents who faithfully modeled church attendance, prayer and generosity.  Ken and Sally’s paths eventually crossed at Greenville University in southern Illinois, where they met and fell in love. They went on to build a life centered around family, faith and service. Ken spent his career as a teacher and coach while Sally worked as an accountant, and together they raised two children. Now retired, they’ve moved to be closer to their children and grandchildren, giving them a new opportunity to pour into the next generation. Through all those years and seasons, the faith Ken and Sally had seen modeled by their families continued to shape their home. Early in their marriage, Ken and Sally met a mentor who encouraged the couple to go deeper with their faith — to study Scripture, ask questions and wrestle honestly with what they believed. It was an important season of discovering that the faith that had been passed down from their families could also become something they personally owned and lived out together. What Do You Take for Granted? Years later, the couple experienced an aha moment when they were introduced to Wycliffe at an event. There, Ken and Sally heard story after story from people who had received Scripture in their own languages. Something clicked for Sally: “We’ve never known a day where we couldn’t access the Bible. And these people have just longed for it, and they’re finally getting it.” For the first time, something that had always surrounded the couple became visible — and it was a gift they could no longer take for granted . Ken and Sally had spent years thinking about the importance of God’s Word. Seeing people receive Scripture in their own languages helped them understand just how extraordinary that access is. “The power of salvation comes through that,” Ken said. “I can’t think of … [a more] important work than providing God’s Word to everybody in the world.” Sally agreed. “To have His Word is as if we’re hearing the voice of God,” she said. “God works through His Word.” This conviction — for people around the world to be able to access Scripture for themselves — became one of the reasons Ken and Sally prioritized a place in their giving for Wycliffe. But it also became part of a larger question about generosity they had been asking themselves for years: “If everything we have is a gift from God, what does it look like to live generously with it?” A Generous Heart Generosity, like faith, was something Ken and Sally had grown up around. Ken remembers his dad giving him money to put in the offering plate, and Sally remembers watching her parents give not just to their church but to people and organizations in need. Sally’s father especially enjoyed giving anonymously. As Ken and Sally have grown older, they’ve learned that generosity isn’t simply about giving a certain percentage or checking a box; it’s about continually asking what it means to have a generous heart . For Ken, the question of what it means to be generous has become what he calls “Kingdom Advancement Giving.” When contemplating giving, he asks, “Is this going to advance the Kingdom for God’s glory?” That question has shaped the way the couple thinks about which individuals and organizations they

title: Wycliffe’s Scott Ross Wants Local U.S. Churches To Join In Global Bible Translation Effort
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Your church can help bring God’s Word to people still waiting. Wycliffe’s Scott Ross shares how prayer, service and initiatives like Adopt a Verse connect local congregations with Bible translation around the world.   The post  Wycliffe’s Scott Ross Wants Local U.S. Churches To Join In Global Bible Translation Effort  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: How old were you when you first learned that Jesus loves you? Perhaps you’ve always known it and can’t remember a day when you didn’t know the song “Jesus Loves Me” or couldn’t recite John 3:16 by heart. Maybe you were a teenager and learned about Jesus’ love through a friend or church summer camp. Or were in college and went to a concert where the gospel was clearly articulated. Maybe you were in the trenches of the workforce, and a coworker boldly shared with you about the God who radically changed their life. Regardless of how old you were, each of us who has chosen to follow Jesus has an origin story — a moment in our lives when the knowledge that “Jesus loves me, this I know, for the Bible tells me so” moved from head knowledge to heart belief. And from then on, our lives were transformed forever. This is the truth of the gospel and the power of understanding that Jesus loves you. People around the world are discovering the personal truth of John 3:16 for themselves in a language and format they clearly understand. Explore why understanding that “God so loved the world” transforms entire communities → A Changing Reality Throughout Christian history, the gospel has spread from one community to the next. Stories were told and retold, Scripture was translated, churches were planted, and discipleship deepened as people learned more about Jesus. Bible translation is foundational to all ministries of the church. It fuels evangelism, church planting, discipleship and more. It equips people to move from a blurry picture of who God is to a clear understanding and personal encounter with Jesus as Lord. Through Scripture, people are able to read, hear or see the love of God on display. Just two decades ago, most of the world’s language communities still needed Bible translation work to begin , let alone be completed. But praise God, in the last few years, we’ve seen tremendous progress made, with Bible translation underway in more languages than ever before . While the change in numbers is exciting, what’s more important is what they signify: Every number represents a person who has a story that matters to God. For these communities, the stories of future generations are being completely rewritten as children will now grow up never remembering a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. That statement bears repeating: There will now be people who never remember a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. From the first word of Genesis to the last word of Revelation, the Bible tells one incredible story: God’s love for the world and His invitation for people from every nation and language to know Him. Get a glimpse of how God continues writing this story today as more and more people are experiencing the power of His Word. Watch the video → A New Generation Growing Up With God’s Word Let’s take a look at some of the recent communities that are experiencing not only life transformation but generational transformation as they encounter Jesus personally through Scripture. Jakalteko | Guatemala The Jakalteko Bible was dedicated in July 2026 in Guatemala! During the celebration, John 1:1-18 was read aloud — a passage that focuses on Christ, the eternal Word and our Redeemer. Early on, many women in the community memorized Job 19 . Like Job, they had faced various hardships in their lives and identified with his suffering. The book reminded them that God remains in control and that, in the midst of difficult circumstances, their Redeemer will deliver them and comfort them in their pain. Today, they have the full counsel of God’s Word and can now see this Redeemer fulfilled in Jesus in the New Testament. They are overjoyed that the Bible has arrived in the language they were born into! When the Bible was distributed, one mother who is raising her family alone said with joy and tears: “Thank God we have the Bible in our language. Now
author: James Buettner

title: 5 Ways to Pray for Bible Translation Around the World
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Prayer is essential to Bible translation. Explore five specific ways to pray for local churches, translation teams and communities around the world.   The post  5 Ways to Pray for Bible Translation Around the World  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Before His ascension to heaven, Jesus called the whole Church to “go and make disciples of all the nations” ( Matthew 28:18, NLT ), a command often referred to now as the Great Commission. God’s plan was to build His Kingdom in and through the Church, including local churches in every corner of the globe. And that’s exactly what’s happening today! God is on the move, and His Spirit is being poured out upon the earth in ways we’ve never seen before, particularly in the history of Bible translation. For so long, the Church was viewed as having the deepest roots and strongest influence in the West, with the West sending out Bible translators to the farthest reaches of the world. But over the last half century, the Church has exploded, expanding South and East and shifting the landscape of Bible translation with it. Johnstone Ndunde, executive director of SIL Global, a key partner of Wycliffe’s, shared: “In the world where we serve, we have many churches that have discipled, educated people [who] are able to serve the Lord as well. God’s mission is no longer from the West to the rest. It is from everyone to everywhere.” “God’s mission is no longer from the West to the rest. It is from everyone to everywhere.” This is God’s hand at work. He desires for people from every language and community to experience His redemptive power through the blood of Jesus, leading to life transformation. Scripture in a language and format they clearly understand plays a vital role in that, enabling them to know God more deeply and grow through discipleship. Today, as the Great Commission is being advanced by the global Church, local churches are taking ownership and linking arms with Wycliffe and other Bible translation agencies around the world to ensure that their communities, countries and even entire regions have God’s Word. Prayer is foundational to seeing God’s Word translated and made accessible to every person still waiting. Whether you’re praying for local churches, translation teams or communities, your prayers matter. Here are five ways you can pray for Bible translation today: Pray for Local Churches and Bible Translation Partnerships Pray for Wisdom and Strength for Bible Translation Teams Pray for Deaf Communities to Encounter Jesus Through Sign Language Pray for More People to Join the Work of Bible Translation Pray for the Translation of the Full Bible 1. Pray for Local Churches and Bible Translation Partnerships As a result of missions and technology, the gospel has spread to more communities than ever before, and now local churches worldwide are rising up to establish evangelism, discipleship, church planting and other activities in their own communities — with Bible translation central to all of those efforts! As local churches work with Bible translation organizations to translate Scripture for their own communities, that partnership is accelerating the pace of the work. This shift to local church ownership is a direct answer to decades of faithful prayer and service. Praise God! PRAY WITH US Heavenly Father, Thank You for how You are raising up men and women who not only love You but who want to be part of sharing the gospel in their own communities, countries and regions. Your love is capturing more people as they encounter You personally in a language and format they clearly understand. Equip local churches to spread Your light and love to their families and neighbors, drawing people to You through Scripture. Amen. title: Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Rediscover the wonder of Christmas by focusing on God’s faithfulness and the hope found in Jesus.   The post  Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Christmas is supposed to be a season of wonder. Twinkling lights, familiar songs, meaningful traditions and time with people you love can all point toward the joy of celebrating Jesus’ birth. But when your December calendar fills with responsibilities and expectations, weariness can settle in before you realize it. Maybe you remember a time when Christmas felt different. As a child, you may have counted down the days and experienced joy in even the smallest traditions. As an adult, you might find yourself simply trying to catch your breath as you move from one responsibility to the next. In the middle of trying to make Christmas special for everyone else, it can be easy to miss the wonder yourself. But the Christmas story gives you an opportunity to slow down and remember what this season is really about. In Luke 1, before the story of Jesus’ birth begins, you meet people who knew what it meant to wait, wonder and trust that God was at work even when they couldn’t yet see what He was doing. Weary of Waiting Luke’s account of the life of Jesus doesn’t begin with Jesus’ birth; it begins instead with the story of Zechariah, an elderly priest who was tired of waiting. Zechariah had heard promises of Israel’s rescue from oppression and sin his entire life. That future must have seemed out of reach under Rome’s harsh control. But Zechariah and his wife, Elizabeth, also had an unfulfilled personal longing: “They had no children because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and they were both very old” ( Luke 1:7, NLT ). One day, as Zechariah performed his duties in the temple, he was chosen to burn incense in the sanctuary — a rare honor with an unexpected result: While Zechariah was in the sanctuary, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the incense altar. Zechariah was shaken and overwhelmed with fear when he saw him. But the angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Zechariah! God has heard your prayer. Your wife, Elizabeth, will give you a son, and you are to name him John. You will have great joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the eyes of the Lord. He must never touch wine or other alcoholic drinks. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth. And he will turn many Israelites to the Lord their God. He will be a man with the spirit and power of Elijah. He will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and he will cause those who are rebellious to accept the wisdom of the godly” ( Luke 1:11-17, NLT ). Trusting God in the Waiting An angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah and announced that God had heard his prayer. Elizabeth would have a son named John who would “… prepare the people for the coming of the Lord” ( Luke 1:17b, NLT ). After years of waiting, God answered Zechariah and Elizabeth’s prayer as part of an even bigger story: They would finally have the child they had prayed for, and their son would prepare the way for Jesus. But Zechariah struggled to understand how it could possibly happen: “… ‘How can I be sure this will happen? I’m an old man now, and my wife is also well along in years’” ( Luke 1:18, NLT ). Zechariah could only see what seemed possible based on his circumstances. But God was asking him to trust what He had promised. The angel Gabriel responded by telling Zechariah that he would be unable to speak until the child was born, adding, “For my words will certainly be fulfilled at the proper time” ( Luke 1:20b, NLT ). Maybe you know what it’s like to pray about something for months or even years. It can be hard to keep trusting that God is working when it seems like nothing is changing. Zechariah’s story reminds us that even when we can’t see what God is doing, He is still faithful to His promises. Waiting is woven throughout the Christmas story. Maybe it’s part of your story too. title: No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: See how Bible translation helps communities access more of God’s Word through print, audio and sign language Scripture today.   The post  No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Imagine reading a book, watching a show or listening to a podcast when suddenly the story just stops mid-sentence. Maybe the previous reader has ripped out a page, the series was canceled before the showrunners could wrap up the plotline, or the producer distributed the episode before realizing it was incomplete. How incredibly frustrating to not experience the full story from start to finish! It can leave us emotionally unsettled, frustrated or even distraught, because at our core, we desire completion. We want to know how things start and how they end. We don’t just want a taste, because it feels like a tease. We’re left wanting more . And we’re not alone in that desire! The same is true for communities around the world who are still waiting for the full counsel of God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. For some, they’re still waiting for the first verse of Scripture to be translated into their language. Others might have a few verses, chapters or Scripture portions . Still others are blessed with a complete New Testament but are waiting for the Old Testament so they can understand everything from Genesis to Revelation. They get a teaser of God’s great story — perhaps enough to understand who Jesus is and that He died for them — but they don’t have the full context as to why His sacrifice was so significant. The Bible changes everything, and together with our partners, Wycliffe believes that everyone should have access to the whole of Scripture. But don’t just take our word for it! Explore these Bible translation stories from our friends around the world who have personally experienced individual and community transformation as a result of encountering God through His Word. Want a glimpse of what it’s like to only have a portion of God’s Word? This “H ly B bl: Incomplete Scriptures” digital booklet helps you see what it’s like to have gaps in your understanding of the Bible. Explore the booklet → The Full “Outfit” of God’s Word Caroline always had access to a Bible growing up. But watching the Chonyi people of Kenya receive the New Testament in their language refreshed her passion for Bible translation, a mission she’s actively engaged in through SIL Kenya, a partner of Wycliffe. “They took a couple of Bibles, wrapped them up like a child,” she shared. “And there was a woman who was carrying the [Bibles]. And they were swinging and dancing, lifting up the [Bibles] and saying, ‘This is our child.’ Calling people, ‘Come,” in the Chonyi language. ‘Come and celebrate the child that has been born in us.’ “That is how the Chonyi people have taken the Bible — the New Testament — in their own language. That it is their child and they’re taking it seriously, making it bear fruit.” People gathered to hear Scripture read in their language, Bible studies began and the impact spread: 300 adults and 50 children gave their lives to Christ! At the celebration, the local pastors shared that now that the New Testament is complete, it’s like they have a shirt. But a shirt isn’t enough; they want a pair of pants (the Old Testament) to complete the outfit! Now work is underway to translate the Old Testament into Chonyi so that they can have the full “outfit” of God’s Word. Praise God! Watch how the Chonyi community celebrated the dedication of the New Testament in their community! As her neighbors listened alongside her, they became captivated by the story of Jesus. One day, someone from the community called the local translation office with a request. “We have been enjoying this Jesus story from this elderly woman, and now it has broken. So could you please send this device so that we could finish the whole story?” The translation team happily sent a new one, and found out that some of the people in th

title: When Generosity Becomes Worship
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Discover how Millie anchored herself in God’s Word during difficult circumstances — and how that shapes her view of generosity.   The post  When Generosity Becomes Worship  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: What circumstances or experiences have shaped your life? For 93-year-old Millie (name changed), her testimony was shaped by the Great Depression and deep loss, but also by an enduring faith and a lifetime of seeing God’s faithfulness unfold. Every chapter of her story points back to the same truth: God’s Word sustained her. Millie was only six weeks old when her father suffered severe burns to his legs from an explosion. Overnight, Millie’s mother found herself caring for a newborn and a toddler while tending to a husband who was facing a long and painful recovery. Life was uncertain, and every dollar mattered. Yet when Millie looks back on those difficult years, she doesn’t first remember hardship. She remembers the faith that was demonstrated. Every Sunday morning, Millie’s mother would reach into a small jar where she saved a few quarters and hand one to Millie and one to her sister before they left for church. The family didn’t have much, but her parents believed that honoring God was never dependent on how much they had. “We were taught to tithe,” Millie recalled. “To give to the Lord because of His goodness to us.” Long before Millie understood phrases like “stewardship” or “planned giving,” she was learning a lesson that would shape the rest of her life: Generosity isn’t born out of abundance; it grows from trusting the one who provides. See how God is using the generosity of one group of friends to impact Bible translation → The Scripture Millie Carried Through the Years As Millie grew older, that foundation of faith continued to guide her. She married a godly man, and they centered their efforts around family, teaching and serving others. Both were educators, and they poured themselves into the lives of children while also remaining deeply involved in their church and community. Together, the couple experienced the joys of raising a family. But they also walked through a devastating loss. While Millie was pregnant with their younger son, the couple’s 7-year-old daughter tragically died. It’s difficult to imagine the depth of grief that Millie endured. Through her pain, she turned to God and His Word for comfort. Even now, decades later, she is still anchored by the promises found in Scripture. One particular passage resonates with Millie deeply: You will keep in perfect peace all who trust in you, all whose thoughts are fixed on you! Trust in the LORD always, for the LORD GOD is the eternal Rock. — Isaiah 26:3-4 (NLT) For Millie, Scripture was what met her in her grief, strengthened her through suffering and continued to anchor and guide her throughout the next chapters of her life. This past Easter, Mille’s family experienced another tragic event — her son was involved in a head-on collision. Thankfully he survived but was hospitalized and treated for serious injuries. Millie believes the Lord’s presence was unmistakable in the moments that followed this event. A Gift Rooted in Gratitude Not long after her son’s accident, Millie received a mailing from Wycliffe Foundation that included information about charitable gift annuities. For Millie, this felt like an invitation and an opportunity to respond to God’s faithfulness through generosity. A charitable gift annuity was not a completely new concept to Millie. Through family members connected with Faith Comes By Hearing (a Wycliffe partner organization), she learned about this unique giving option and appreciated that it could provide her with a lifetime income while also supporting a ministry she cared deeply about. When she received the information about charitable gift annuities, she saw it as another opportunity to worship the Lord and express her gratitude for His protection and provision. Millie reached out to Wycliffe Foundation, and Michael Occhipinti, senior gift planning advisor, quickly connected with her. He walked alongside her throughout the process as she prayerfully considered her next step. For Millie, establishing a charitable gift annuity became ano

title: Good News for Midlife
summary: A review of Jared Wilson’s Good News for Midlife, a candid, gospel-centered guide for men in middle age. See Also A La Carte (May 2) A La Carte (March 28) Weekend A La Carte (June 12)
content: I will be turning 50 in a few weeks’ time, and whatever else that may mean, it definitely means that I am now well into middle age. Now that I’m here, I feel like there were many resources to guide me when I was a young man, and there will be many to guide me as I become an old man , but not nearly so much that pertain to these middle years. Jared Wilson seems to have noticed this as well, and he did something about it by writing Good News for Midlife: Navigating Middle Age with Guts and Grace . Good News for Midlife Jared Wilson Buy from Amazon (Affiliate links) Midlife is a strange season in that we are neither young nor old. We are no longer just starting out, but we are also not yet near the end. While our work is well underway, we have not yet brought it to completion, and though we may see the end on the distant horizon, we are still in the game and still have a lot to offer. In its own way, it is a time that can be embraced or resented, that can be full of victories or full of failures. For some men, these will be the best of years, and for some they will be the worst. Wilson describes the season this way in his introduction: As men reach middle age, we face unique challenges related to physical and spiritual health, reckoning with our past, and preparing for retirement or the future in general. But while this season of life poses unique challenges in marriage, family, and health—not to mention in our thoughts about legacy, heritage, and “what it’s all about”—midlife also presents exciting opportunities to trust Jesus for personal, marital, and spiritual flourishing. Wilson has written this book for men who understand there will be new challenges and new blessings in these years and who wish to remain faithful throughout them. It is for men who want guidance as they approach these years and enter them, lest they fail to make them all they could be. To that end, he divides his book into two broad sections. In the first, he explains how to flourish now. He writes about the necessity of keeping the local church central to a man’s life since “real men are churchmen.” Men need to embrace their position in the life of the church and maintain a full commitment to it. He writes about marriage in the middle years as children gain their independence and the house grows empty. “The midlife marriage season—whether you’ve got older kids at home or you’re living together in that empty nest—is one that has proven challenging for countless couples. Many husbands and wives spend twenty years or more gradually relating to each other only as dad and mom, and when they’re suddenly given more time together, they don’t have any idea what to do with it. They look at each other and think, Who are you?” In this way, marriage becomes different from what it was, and wise men will learn to adapt to these changes. Parenting changes too as children no longer need their fathers to function in the ways they did in the little years. “When your children become adults and leave the nest, your role may change even further. You’ve gone from quarterback to coach and now to booster. Boosters wield some influence on the team, but it’s more in the way of support from the background. As many dads of adult children will tell you, they especially feel like an athletic booster in the area of ongoing financial support!” After covering parenting, Wilson covers work, friendship, and health, all areas that may be different in midlife than in other stages, but each of which is important to a man who is eager to embrace this middle stage of life. The book’s second part is a trio of chapters that look to the future and to finishing well. Here Wilson discusses legacy, lament, and endurance. Legacy considers the heritage a man wishes to bequeath to his descendants, lament honestly assesses and repents of failures, and endurance is finishing well, even if that involves finishing physically weak. He wraps it up with a series of very practical ways that men can honor the Lord

summary: Churches shouldn’t just ban Hillsong, Bethel, and Elevation / The new benefit of clergy / Everything sad coming untrue / What do we do with New Testament books not written by apostles? / The million dollar gene editing question / Scrolling the soul shallow / Kindle deals / The funnies See Also Weekend A La Carte (December 27) A La Carte (October 2) A La Carte (November 25)
content: Good morning from San Diego, where I’m speaking at a men’s retreat this weekend. This is my final event for the year, so I guess I’ll soon be settled in at home for the rest of the winter. Sales & Deals Yesterday saw the launch of a huge sale on Kindle books, most of which are published by Crossway. You can find that complete list on my November Kindle Sale page. Many of these books are cheaper now than I’ve ever seen them. Of course, there are some other Kindle deals as well which you can find in the usual place. Westminster Books has a great deal this week on R.C. Sproul’s commentary series . I have often found them useful. Recommended Reading Churches Shouldn’t Just Ban Hillsong, Bethel, and Elevation. Though I’m sticking with my perspective on the matter, I appreciate Kenny Klinglesmith’s alternative take on singing Hillsong, Bethel, and Elevation. “I’ve been leading worship for 15 years. For the past 10, I’ve served as a contract leader for multiple congregations throughout Texas. And increasingly, I’ve encountered churches all across denominational lines taking a strong position: They won’t sing songs written by the worship behemoths Hillsong, Bethel, or Elevation.” The New Benefit of Clergy. Writing especially of Russell Brand and David Walliams, Carl Trueman compares modern celebrity scandals to older clergy scandals. “Reviewing the autobiography of Salvador Dalí, George Orwell asked why moral monsters like the Spanish surrealist were granted immunity from accepted moral standards. His answer was that artists enjoy ‘benefit of clergy’—the medieval practice of granting clergymen accused of crimes the right to be tried in church courts, where penalties were considerably lighter than those faced by ordinary villains. The same holds true today. We grant our modern holy men, the artists and entertainers, a similar privilege…” (You’ll need one of your per-browser monthly allotment of free articles to read it.) Everything Sad Coming Untrue. “Gandalf! I thought you were dead! But then I thought I was dead myself. Is everything sad going to come untrue? What’s happened to the world?” Jacob Crouch explains why this little scene from The Lord of the Rings chokes him up. What Do We Do With New Testament Books Not Written by Apostles? Not all of the New Testament books were written by apostles, of course. Some people suggest this presents a problem when it comes to their authority or place in the canon. Michael Kruger disagrees. “In the end, it is fair to say that the entire 27-book corpus of the New Testament is apostolic . In some fashion, they all bear official apostolic testimony about Jesus and his message. Thus, they all bear the very authority of Jesus himself.” The Million Dollar Gene Editing Question. Emma Waters outlines two different forms of gene editing and explains why she regards them very differently. “In many of our conversations about technology, the question is rarely whether to ban a tool outright. The goal is to figure out how to use it for health, healing, and human flourishing, while banning or limiting the ways it can be misused.” This, she says, is the case with gene editing. Scrolling the Soul Shallow. John Piper does a good job of explaining what it means to have a shallow soul. “I have said many times that the worst problem with television (or now let’s just say Instagram or any online media in general) is probably not the pervasive sexualization of all of life — that’s big enough — but rather the pervasive trivialization of all of life. You can scarcely watch TV ads or be online for more than ten seconds without being dump-trucked with banality and silliness. Grown men and women, even famous grown men and women, act like eleven-year-olds whose high point at summer camp was to bob for apples in a toilet filled with Mello Yello — the apex of satisfaction. That’s the quality that we’re being dumped on every day.” The Funnies My friend Chris Martin maintains a Substack called The Funnies , and every Saturda
